# TManage — implementation status

Status vocabulary is fixed by `15-AI-EXECUTION-HANDBOOK.md` §6:
`not_started` · `designed` · `design_validated` · `contract_defined` · `implemented` ·
`tested` · `release_ready` · `released`.

A row is only `tested` if a check was **actually executed** and its result recorded below.

## 2026-09-20 — FR-05 Approvals: persist and decide over a content-hashed version (slice x92)

Built on branch `x92-approvals-decide` (off `master` after pass 11, `d6ccc9a`), **not merged**.
The first vertical slice of the approval aggregate — until now domain-only
(`packages/domain/src/state-machines/approval.ts`) with no persistence and no HTTP. Migration
**`0027_deliverable_versions_and_approvals.sql`** (the base tops out at `0026`, so this is the next
contiguous number — NEXT-SCOPES-5's "0029" assumed x90/x91 had landed first, which they have not on
this base) creates two tenant-scoped tables: immutable `deliverable_versions` (id, org, project,
deliverable ref, `content_hash`, creator; INSERT-only, a trigger refuses any UPDATE) and append-only
`approvals` (bound version + captured `content_hash`, `state` from `APPROVAL_STATES`, `reviewer_ids`,
`policy`, `decided_by_user_id`/`decided_at`/`feedback`; a trigger refuses re-deciding a terminal row
and refuses a decision without actor+time or a `changes_requested` without feedback). New module
`apps/api/src/modules/approvals/` (module/controller/service + two repositories). **Authorization is
object-layer, not a route guard:** `approval.decide`/`approval.read`/`deliverable.*` stay in
`UNGUARDED_CAPABILITIES` and out of `GUARDED_OPERATIONS`; the decide route carries the coarse
`@RequireCapability('approval.read')` (UX only, mirroring `moderateMessage`→`conversation.read`) and
the service calls `authorize()` with the loaded row — `deliverable.review` (internal-only) to open
and `approval.decide` with `isAssignedReviewer` from `reviewer_ids` to decide (AUTH-08). The decide
transaction re-checks the captured hash against the deliverable's current governed version
(`contentHashEquals`) and moves the approval to `invalidated` on a mismatch rather than deciding
(INT-16/INT-17); a decided approval records the immutable actor, time and hash (US-C03).
CONTRACT-001 `ApprovalDecisionView` is authored API-only and exempted in `scripts/contracts-check.mjs`
(no web consumer this slice — x92-b adds the client deep-link screen and projection, x92-c the E2E-05
journey). **Gates green and recorded:** `@tmanage/api` typecheck, the unit project (647 pass, 7 new
approvals cases), `pnpm lint`, `pnpm format:check`, `pnpm contracts:check`. Revert proof on the
decide source proved the AUTH-08 denial and the hash-mismatch invalidation load-bearing (SHA-256
restored byte-identical). **DB proof:** `apps/api/test/approvals-001-decide.db.test.ts` (migration
applies + tenant-scoped open→decide round-trip with the hash re-check + cross-tenant non-resolution)
is written; its execution state is recorded in the x92 report (deferred unless `db-e2e.lock` was
held). Status: `tested` (unit) / DB `implemented`, pending the DB suite.

## 2026-09-19 — USAGE-001 slice 4c, the threshold mail + quiet-hours bypass (slice x74)

Built on branch `x74-usage-threshold-mail` (off x68's HEAD `1526f6b`), **not merged**. Completes
the mail follow-up x68 (slice 4b) recorded: 4b shipped the in-app inbox notice for
`usage.threshold_reached.v1`; this slice adds the email, as the interrupting channel, honouring
NOTIF-001 and INBOX-001.

- **The mail (acceptance §1).** A new `UsageThresholdMailer` (`apps/worker/src/notifications/
usage-threshold-mailer.ts`) and its consumer half `createUsageThresholdMail`
  (`consumers/usage-threshold-mail.ts`), composed in `registry.ts` with x68's notice via
  `both(notice, mail)` — notice first, so a mail throw rolls back an event whose notice is
  re-inserted idempotently on redelivery. It does **not** fork `ClientRequestMailer`'s
  client-request facts: the copy is `35 §1`'s "Storage at 85% — 8.5 GB of 10 GB", rendered from the
  x63 payload (`band/used/reserved/quota`), and, like the credential receipt, carries **no link**
  (the usage screen it would point at is a later slice). One mail per recipient, the same
  owner/org_admin fan-out and the same dedupe-absorbed idempotency as the notice.
- **Preferences (acceptance §2).** Each recipient's `notification_preferences.email_enabled` is
  read at delivery (`findUsageMailRecipient`, a `LEFT JOIN` so a person with no row is
  default-reachable per `0022`) and a recipient who turned the mail channel off is skipped; the
  in-app notice stays unconditional (x68). **Divergence, recorded:** the existing relay mailers
  (client-request, credential-change) do not read `email_enabled` — their recipients are external
  client users / security receipts where the toggle does not apply — so this is the first consumer
  to honour it. It is read in the same in-transaction, re-resolved, default-reachable style the
  quiet-hours read uses, which is the "exactly as the existing mail consumers honour them" the
  brief names; honouring an explicit opt-out (with the canonical in-app channel still reaching the
  owner) was taken as the safer reading of §2 than leaving the toggle unhonoured.
- **Quiet hours + band-100 bypass (acceptance §3).** Bands 70/85/95 defer through the existing
  INBOX-001 mechanism; band 100 (uploads already blocked — critical) bypasses. The type-keyed
  `QUIET_HOURS_BYPASS_EVENT_TYPES` cannot express a per-band rule, so the smallest generic
  extension was added in the domain: `eventBypassesQuietHours(type, payload)` consults the type set
  and then a payload-predicate registry `QUIET_HOURS_BYPASS_PAYLOAD_PREDICATES` keyed by event type
  (`usage.threshold_reached.v1 → band === 100`). The type-only `eventTypeBypassesQuietHours` is
  unchanged for the client-request path. **Divergence, recorded:** a fan-out has per-recipient
  windows, so a deferred recipient is re-enqueued as their **own** `QUIET_HOURS_MAIL_RESUME_TYPE`
  row (the envelope gained an optional `recipientUserId`); the resume mails just that one recipient,
  because re-running the whole fan-out on resume would re-mail the recipients who were not in quiet
  hours. The resume type now carries both the client-request and usage resume handlers, composed
  with `both` (each no-ops on a row that is not its `originalType`).
- **Failure isolation (acceptance §4).** One `afterCommit` effect is staged per recipient, so the
  dispatcher's per-effect `try/catch` isolates a failed send, and `mailer.deliver` also never
  throws (absorb-and-report, matching the two existing relay mailers). A mail failure for one
  recipient rolls back neither the committed inbox notice nor the other recipients' mails.
- **Gates.** `pnpm --filter @tmanage/worker test` 135 passed (was 128); `@tmanage/domain` test 147
  passed; `pnpm lint`, `pnpm format:check`, `pnpm contracts:check` (26 views, 16 paired) and
  `pnpm build:worker` green. No new API `*View` and no new catalog event (the resume type is
  worker-internal, like `CREDENTIAL_CHANGE_NOTICE_TYPE`), so no contract entry was needed. No DB
  test written: the consumer reads two tables and writes one, all proven through the fakes; the
  end-to-end path against MySQL is UNPROVEN here (no `db-e2e.lock`).

## 2026-09-19 — USAGE-001 slice 3, reconciled counters (slice x53)

Built on branch `x53-usage-001-reconcile` (off x48's approved HEAD `573b5ec`), **not merged**.
The reconciler that closes the loop the append-only ledger (slice 2) opened: per organization,
sum `usage_ledger_entries` per counter under the counter row's own lock, compare with
`usage_counters`, and on drift repair the counter **towards the ledger** — the ledger is the
source of truth (`49-PRICING` §6), so this pass never writes it.

- New `apps/api/src/modules/files/usage-reconciler.ts` — the pure `reconcileCounter(counter,
ledger)` diff (unit-tested) plus the `UsageReconciler` job. Per organization, in one
  transaction: `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` the counter (CONC-06, so no reserve/commit/release moves
  it under the read), sum the ledger, and either correct + bump `version` + stamp
  `reconciled_at` + write one audit row on drift, or stamp `reconciled_at` alone when clean.
  `reconciled_at` (the column exists since 0015 and nothing wrote it) is written on **every**
  run. Cross-tenant scan is the audited escape hatch the expiry sweeper uses, read-only,
  allowlisted to `usage_counters`.
- `usage-ledger.repository.ts` gains `sumByCounter` (the slice's one read of the ledger);
  `usage-counters.repository.ts` gains `organizationsWithCounter`, `lockForReconcile`,
  `correct` (version-conditional), and `touchReconciledAt`.
- `packages/domain/src/policies/audit.ts` adds the `usage_counter.drift_corrected` action
  (`object_type` `usage_counter`, actor null — the system case, as an expiry's row is).
- Wired like the sweeper: `USAGE_RECONCILER` token, a `FilesModule` provider built on the same
  counters/ledger/audit, entry point `apps/api/src/reconcile.ts` (`--once`) and a
  `reconcile:once` script. **Now scheduled (slice x56, below):** `reconcile:once` is on the
  deployment's cron mechanism — its own hourly entry in the runbooks — and in
  `e2e/setup/stack.ts`, so `reconciled_at` is written outside a manual run.

**Divergence from the pre-build note (recorded, not a defect).** The USAGE-001 pre-build note
for slice 3 (this file, "Reconciled counters") named "a correcting ledger row and an audit row
on drift". The brief supersedes that: the ledger is the source of truth, so a correcting ledger
row would make the check circular (it would edit the very thing being reconciled against). This
slice therefore writes **only** an audit row on drift and corrects the counter to the ledger
sum, never the ledger. Under Peter's delegation (2026-09-05: take the recommended option).

The database suite that would prove it (`apps/api/test/usage-001-reconcile.db.test.ts`, four
acceptance cases: drift corrected, `reconciled_at` written, no-drift no-op, tenant isolation) is
written and **unexecuted** (no `mysqld` this run; this agent does not own `db-e2e.lock`). The
pure diff is proven by `usage-reconciler.test.ts` (unit, executed).

## 2026-09-19 — INBOX-001: quiet hours honoured in delivery (slice x57)

Run `claude-auto-1789805818`, branch `x57-inbox-001-quiet-hours` off x54's `f3647f1`,
implemented by **Claude Opus 4.8**. x54 stored the quiet-hours columns; this slice reads them at
the delivery seam so an interrupting channel actually waits.

**What is built.** A pure module `packages/domain/src/notifications/quiet-hours.ts`:
`isInQuietHours(now, prefs)` (handles a window inside a day, a window crossing midnight, and the
recipient's IANA zone via `Intl` — no new dependency), `quietHoursResumeAt(now, prefs)` (the
window's next end, the instant a deferred delivery resumes), `eventTypeBypassesQuietHours(type)`
with `QUIET_HOURS_BYPASS_EVENT_TYPES` (the `24-EVENT-CATALOG` §4 `yes-critical` kinds —
`09-MVP-PRD`'s "critical security events" that interrupt regardless), and `isValidTimeZone`.

**Where it hooks in.** The interrupting channel today is client-request **email**, staged in
`apps/worker/src/consumers/client-request-mail.ts` via `effects.afterCommit`. Before staging,
the mail consumer reads the recipient's window (`findRecipientQuietHours`) and, if the submitter
is inside it and the event type is not urgent, defers: it re-enqueues the delivery as a **dedicated
internal event type** `notification.quiet_hours_resume.v1` (`enqueueQuietHoursMailResume`, existing
`outbox_events` table — no migration) with `available_at` = the window's end and stages nothing
this pass. The resume row's payload wraps the original event's type and payload. The in-app
notification the composed notification consumer wrote stays committed, so
`35-NOTIFICATION-AND-EMAIL-COPY` §1's canonical channel arrives at once and only the email waits.
When the resume row is claimed the dispatcher routes it — by type — to the resume handler alone
(`createQuietHoursMailResume`, keyed only in `registry.ts` when a transport is configured), which
recovers the mail kind from the wrapped original type and sends unconditionally, so a deferral is a
single hop. Urgent (`yes-critical`) kinds are never deferred. None of those kinds has a producer
yet, so the bypass is proven only by unit test.

**Design fragility closed (x57 review "Important").** The first cut re-enqueued the resume with the
_original_ event type plus a payload marker, so no-double-delivery rested on every consumer of that
type being marker-aware or idempotent — true today (the notification consumer is idempotent via
`uq_notifications_dedupe`, the mail consumer read the marker), but a future non-marker-aware
`client_request.*` consumer added to the registry would have double-fired on the resume row. The
dedicated type removes that implicit contract: the resume row is a different type, routed to the
resume handler alone, so ordinary consumers never see it. The marker (`QUIET_HOURS_RESUME_MARKER` /
`isQuietHoursResume`) is gone. The type follows `24-EVENT-CATALOG`'s naming convention but is a
worker-internal delivery-mechanism type (like `CREDENTIAL_CHANGE_NOTICE_TYPE`), so it is
deliberately **not** a member of the domain `OUTBOX_EVENT_CATALOG`; `outbox_events.type` is a free
`VARCHAR` with no allow-list, and no producer or consumer of it exists outside the worker.

**The x54 Minor, closed.** The `PUT` route now validates `quietHoursTimezone` as a real IANA zone
(`isValidTimeZone`) and rejects a start without an end or an end without a start.

**Not in scope, stated per the brief.** Honouring channel opt-outs (`in_app_enabled`,
`email_enabled`) and per-kind opt-outs — not applied when this slice landed; digests — still not
applied; any migration — none, the columns already exist. **Update (x74):** the usage-threshold mail
path now reads `email_enabled` and skips an opted-out recipient
(`apps/worker/src/consumers/usage-threshold-mail.ts:125,162`); `in_app_enabled`, per-kind opt-outs
and digests remain unapplied at delivery.

**Tests.** `packages/domain/src/notifications/quiet-hours.test.ts` (window inside a day, crossing
midnight, timezone offset, no window, the urgent bypass, the resume time) and one route case added
to `notification-preferences.controller.test.ts` (bad timezone → 400), both in unit projects. The
handler-registry suite (`work-item-lifecycle.test.ts`) gains one focused case pinning that the
resume type routes to a dedicated handler, not to the notification consumer. The worker deferral
(re-enqueue + resume against real rows) is still **UNPROVEN**: it is exercised only against a live
DB / outbox loop, which this slice does not own (`db-e2e.lock`); no DB test was added because the
routing is proven structurally by the unit case and the pure decision by the domain suite, and a
DB case would not run here.

## 2026-09-19 — NOTIF-001 second half: the preferences table (slice x54)

Run `claude-auto-1789791408`, branch `x54-notif-001-preferences` off `master` `a204ebe`,
implemented by **Claude Opus 4.8**. NOTIF-001's first half deliberately stopped short of
preferences because `contracts/tmanage-core.dbml` drew no table and building one "would
outrun the contract" (see "NOTIF-001 first half" below). This slice is the storage that half
was waiting on.

**What is built.** `0022_notification_preferences.sql` creates a per-`(organization_id,
user_id)` table with the two delivery channels `24-EVENT-CATALOG` §2 has (`in_app_enabled`,
`email_enabled`, both on by default), the digest window TM-27 names
(`digest_frequency` ENUM `off`|`daily`|`weekly`, default `off` = immediate), and the
quiet-hours columns INBOX-001 needs (`quiet_hours_start`/`_end` TIME, `quiet_hours_timezone`
VARCHAR(64), all nullable). A read/upsert repository (`notification-preferences.repository.
ts`), a service that returns defaults when no row exists (`notification-preferences.service.
ts`, `DEFAULT_NOTIFICATION_PREFERENCES`), a caller's-own `GET`/`PUT` route under
`v1/organizations/:orgSlug/notification-preferences` guarded by `work.read` (the capability
INBOX-001 chose, for the same reasons — the route reads `principal.userId` only, never a path
value), the `tmanage_app` `INSERT, UPDATE` grant (no DELETE), the `schema.ts` mirror, and the
`TENANT_TABLES` registration.

**Interpretation recorded as a divergence.** The brief said "the channels/kinds 24 names".
`24-EVENT-CATALOG` names notification-triggering event _types_ (the "kinds") but draws no
per-kind preference matrix, and `22-SCREEN-BY-SCREEN` TM-27 — the actual settings surface —
enumerates exactly "notification channels, quiet hours, digest". This table stores those and
**does not** model a per-event-type opt-out matrix; adding one would invent a contract shape
neither document draws. If per-kind granularity is wanted, it is a later contract decision.

**Not in scope, and stated so here per the brief.** Honouring these preferences in delivery —
the bundler/relay reading this table to suppress, defer or batch a notification — is a later
slice. This slice stores settings; the rest — channel and per-kind opt-outs, digests — is not yet
read to change what is delivered. Quiet hours, though, are now applied by INBOX-001 (slice x57,
dated section above).

**Tests.** `apps/api/test/notif-001-preferences.db.test.ts` (defaults on first read, upsert
round-trip and single-row replacement, user isolation within a studio, organization isolation
with the user id held constant) — **UNEXECUTED**: this slice does not own `db-e2e.lock`. Route
authentication and own-only scoping are a unit test,
`apps/api/src/modules/notifications/notification-preferences.controller.test.ts` (401 for an
anonymous caller through the real `SessionAuthGuard`, 200 with the caller's own preferences),
which runs in the api unit project. Status: **implemented**; `tested` awaits the DB suite.

### x4 — line endings decided by `.gitattributes`, not `core.autocrlf` (branch `x4-gitattributes-lf`, not merged)

Folded from the former `docs/x4-status-entry.md`, now deleted. Every checkout here carries
`core.autocrlf=true` while `.prettierrc.json` sets `"endOfLine": "lf"`, and nothing reconciled the
two: a clean `git merge` wrote merged files back as CRLF so `pnpm format:check` failed on files
nobody edited; a fresh `git worktree add` came out with 671 tracked text files CRLF, reddening the
format gate before any work; the main checkout showed ~84 phantom-dirty files byte-identical to the
index; and reports had acquired a standing "format:check fails at base" exception that hides a real
failure when one appears. The fix is a root `.gitattributes` with baseline `* text=auto eol=lf`,
every tracked binary format enumerated from `git ls-files` and marked with Git's `binary` macro
(108 `.png`, 24 `.ttf`, 12 each `.woff2`/`.woff`/`.eot`, 10 `.otf`, 3 each `.webp`/`.jpg`, and
`docs/design/source/project/.thumbnail`), `*.bat`/`*.cmd` pinned `eol=crlf` and `*.sh`/`*.bash`,
`pnpm-lock.yaml` and `*.sql` pinned LF for stated forward-looking reasons. A `.gitattributes` does
not renormalise an existing working tree: each checkout's owner runs, once, on a clean tree,
`git add --renormalize .` (stages nothing — every text blob is already LF), then
`git rm --cached -r -q . && git reset --hard`, then confirms with `git ls-files --eol` and
`pnpm format:check`; no `git config` change is needed because `eol=lf` overrides `core.autocrlf`.
Verified in `next-slices-2026-09-12/` (before: 671 `i/lf w/crlf`; `git add --renormalize` staged
nothing; a scratch clone at this branch came out LF and passed prettier, the same clone at `master`
came out CRLF and failed). **This worktree already carries that `.gitattributes`**, so
`docs/implementation-status.md` is LF here and this sweep's edits stay LF; no database suite is
involved.

`CreatedOrganizationView` in `provisioning.service.ts`; `EnrolledFactorView` in
`authentication.service.ts`; `RealtimeTicketView` in `realtime.controller.ts`), typed at the return
sites with zero change to the response bytes, and the first three paired `Exact`, taking
`contracts:check` to 36 views, 27 paired (26 exact, 1 narrowing), 9 exempt. `RealtimeTicketView`'s
pair is deferred: `RealtimeModule` is providerless so the view has no `*.service.ts` home, and the
coverage guard enumerates service files only until x77 extends it to controller-declared views.

### x13 — the grant script narrows on re-apply, R10 (branch `x13-grant-revokes`, not merged)

Folded into the header and the D07 body above. `scripts/db/users.sql` now issues
`REVOKE ALL PRIVILEGES, GRANT OPTION` against each of `tmanage_app`, `tmanage_worker` and
`tmanage_migrator`, between that principal's `CREATE USER` and its first `GRANT`, and enumerates
each principal's intended set in the file, so `pnpm db:grants` is corrective as well as additive and
idempotent in the strong sense — closing R10 (P1), which reported that the script carried no
`REVOKE` and so left an older installation's database-wide `SELECT`, including over the credential
tables, in force. The upgrade path is proved by **executed** unit tests (`grants.test.ts` 14 cases,
`users-sql.test.ts` amended; api unit 458/458). **The reconciliation that reads the privileges
actually in force on a server and fails on any excess,
`apps/api/test/grant-reconciliation.db.test.ts`, is written but unexecuted** — it needs
`TMANAGE_TEST_GRANT_ADMIN_DATABASE_URL` pointed at a provisioned server, and this machine's
database suite runs as an administrative user, where a missing grant is invisible. Hostinger still
defeats ADR-0001 layer 2 regardless (hPanel grants each MySQL user full privileges while `env.ts`
compares only usernames); `docs/runbooks/deploy.md` was not updated for the re-apply window and
should be.

### x14 — the lockout denial of service, C-1 (branch `x14-lockout-dos-defaults`, not merged)

`IDENTITY-SECURITY-AUDIT.md` C-1: the shipped defaults had the per-source-account budget (10) above
the per-user lockout threshold (5), so one address could drive any known account into a 900 s
lockout it could not clear. `RATE_LIMIT_AUTH_MAX_REQUESTS` now defaults to `4` (a named constant
beside `AUTH_MAX_FAILURES_IN_WINDOW`), and `env.ts` refuses at boot, in every environment, any
configuration where the budget is at or above the lockout threshold, with a message naming both
variables. Tests now bind the _shipped_ defaults, not their own literals (config `env.test.ts` +6,
new `api-config.test.ts`; both **executed**, and three SHA-256-verified reverts proved them
load-bearing, including `expected 10 to be less than 5` on the pre-fix defaults). **Honest limit,
recorded here and in `env.ts`:** because the two windows differ (300 s budget vs 900 s lockout) one
address still gets 12 admitted failures per lockout window, so sustained single-address lockout
remains possible; the durable fix (verify-first, throttle only the failing path) is a behaviour
change needing the database lock and is the next item. The added assertions in
`apps/api/test/id-002-credentials.db.test.ts` are type-checked but **written and unexecuted**
(`pnpm --filter @tmanage/api test -- --project database id-002-credentials`). I-1 (no session-revoke
route) and I-3/I-4 (source-key rotation) remain open and multiply what is left of C-1.

### worker / outbox — the two Critical findings (branch `x8-worker-outbox-critical`, not merged)

Folded into the PLAT-004 row below. CRITICAL-1: a handler that _killed the process_ never reached
`recordFailure`, so `attempts` never moved and a poison row could never park — it blocked the whole
queue across restarts. The audit's own smallest fix was one statement short (its extra `UPDATE`
lands inside the batch transaction a crash destroys), so one batch is now two transactions — a
committed **reservation** that increments `attempts` before the handler runs, then the batch —
`recordFailure` no longer touches `attempts`, and the backoff arithmetic is byte-identical.
CRITICAL-2: a dead relay and an idle relay were indistinguishable; `readOutboxBacklog` (oldest
pending age, parked kept out of the age) plus a heartbeat file are exposed as `relay:status` (exit 1
past threshold) and a non-zero `relay:once`, read on the worker's own credential so **no grant
changed**. Proved by **executed** worker unit tests (`claim-attempts.test.ts` 7 cases,
`health.test.ts` 17 cases; worker 71/71) with existing tests unweakened. **The database case that
confirms the reservation commits and the aggregate reads what MySQL stores,
`apps/api/test/plat-004-claim-attempts.db.test.ts` (8 cases), is written but unexecuted**
(`pnpm test:db`), and the existing `plat-004-relay.db.test.ts` under the new `attempts` semantics is
likewise unrun and should be run first. The accepted trade (a crash costs an attempt to every
reserved batch-mate, bounded by `OUTBOX_BATCH_SIZE`) is pinned by a test; IMPORTANT-1..6 and the
Minor findings are untouched. The branch is misnamed `x8-web-shell-findings` in its worktree and
should be renamed for the worker/outbox fix when committed.

## D09 — every proxy forwarding header was trusted: built on a branch

**Finding** (production review of 2026-09-05, `CLAUDE-REVIEW-REPORT.md` §D09, P1 conditional),
as the plan carried it:

> Every proxy forwarding header is trusted. `apps/api/src/main.ts:39` passes `trustProxy: true`
> unconditionally, and `apps/api/src/common/http/fastify-adapter.ts` forwards it to Fastify.
> Local injection reproduced two accepted requests from one socket peer using two different
> forwarded addresses against a one-request-per-address limiter.
>
> Exploitable when the origin is directly reachable, or when the edge preserves
> attacker-controlled forwarding headers. Deployment network configuration was never inspected,
> so this is not a proven production exploit; it is a configuration that cannot be relied on.

D08 raised its priority: while the address was attacker-chosen, both address-keyed budgets of
the sign-in abuse control rotated with it, and one host could present as any number of addresses
and so spend the global budget and refuse everybody's sign-in, MFA, recovery and
re-authentication until the window turned.

**What was built** (branch `d09-trusted-proxy`, cut from `master` `3fed68d`; five commits).

- `22a8072` — **trust is configured, not assumed.** New
  `packages/config/src/trusted-proxies.ts`: `TRUSTED_PROXY_ADDRESSES` is a comma-separated list
  of IPv4/IPv6 addresses and CIDR ranges, parsed into exactly the two shapes Fastify's own
  `trustProxy` takes — `false`, or `string[]` — so there is no second notion of trust in between
  to drift from the operator's. **Unset or blank is trust nobody**, which is the safe default and
  needs no configuration: `request.ip` is then the socket peer and `X-Forwarded-For` is an
  ordinary header. A malformed entry (a name, a stray comma, a `/33`) **fails the boot** naming
  the entry rather than becoming a silent `false`; so does `/0`, by name, because it is
  `trustProxy: true` spelled as a range and would otherwise kill boot from inside
  `@fastify/proxy-addr` with nothing naming the variable. A hop count is deliberately not
  offered: it asserts the shape of a topology rather than its identity. `main.ts` now passes
  `trustProxy: env.TRUSTED_PROXY_ADDRESSES`, and `createFastifyAdapter`'s option carries
  `TrustedProxies` rather than a boolean, defaulting to `false` — so every suite that builds its
  own adapter gets the socket peer unless it says otherwise.
- `4545e6e` — **the request-level proof**, `apps/api/src/common/http/trusted-proxy-requests.test.ts`,
  eight cases, no production code touched. Each drives the whole configured chain the composition
  root drives — a raw environment bag through `loadEnv`, into `createFastifyAdapter`, into
  Fastify, out as `request.ip`, into a control — against the two things production actually keys
  on the address: the part limiter inside the adapter's own octet-stream parser, and D08's
  sign-in abuse control called exactly as `authentication.service.ts` calls it. The finding's own
  reproduction is inverted there: two forwarded addresses from one socket peer are now **one**
  key, the second request is refused, and a genuinely different peer is still admitted. All eight
  fail against the pre-fix tree.
- `0f779fb` — **the untruncated insert D08 carried here** (its follow-up 1).
  `recordAuthenticationEvent` clamps `ip` to 45 and `userAgent` to 255 **by code point** —
  `Array.from`, not `slice`. Clamp rather than
  reject, argued in the file: the insert is on sign-in's failure path, and an over-long value
  under strict mode is `ER_DATA_TOO_LONG`, which loses the audit row that is the only trace of an
  enumeration sweep and turns the refusal into a 500. The database cases failed pre-fix with
  `Data too long for column 'ip'` from the real engine.
- `9101e60` — **the reason for the code-point clamp corrected.** `0f779fb` had argued that a
  UTF-16 `slice` could leave an unpaired surrogate MySQL would refuse as invalid UTF-8 however
  short the value was, so the clamp meant to prevent a failed insert would itself have caused
  one. That is false in this stack, and the branch's own database case now proves it: mysql2
  (3.23.3) maps this connection's `utf8mb4` charset to Node's `'utf8'` encoder, which substitutes
  U+FFFD for an unpaired surrogate before a byte leaves the process, and the server accepts the
  row. The real reasons the clamp counts code points are that the substitution is a
  **normalisation this log is forbidden to make** — the table records what arrived — and that a
  UTF-16 slice also **under-fills the column**, since an astral character is two units and one
  MySQL character. The clamp itself is unchanged; only its justification is, in the source, in
  the unit file's header and in the database docstring that echoed it. Three smaller corrections
  ride along: the lone-surrogate unit case no longer states its expectation as the very `slice`
  the suite argues against, the column-width constants no longer claim the database case keeps
  them in step with the migration in both directions, and `ER_CANT_AGGREGATE` is gone from the
  unit header, where it had been named as if it were an invalid-string error. The final tree has
  **ten unit cases and seven database cases** for the clamp — `0f779fb` had ten and six.
- The **documentation sweep** — this section, and the corrections listed under "What was
  corrected" below. No behaviour, no assertion.

**Gates.** `pnpm build:packages`, `pnpm --filter @tmanage/api typecheck`, `pnpm lint` green at
each commit. The api unit project went 27 files / 419 tests at the base to **29 files / 437
tests**; `@tmanage/config` is **3 files / 117 tests** (`trusted-proxies.test.ts` is 20 of them).
The identity database files ran **2 files / 107 tests** green at `0f779fb`
(`d09-t4-db-identity.log`), against the embedded `mysql-memory-server` MySQL every earlier slice
used. `9101e60` added a seventh clamp case, so that count is superseded: the re-run after it
covered the one file the commit touched, `id-002-credentials.db.test.ts`, at **1 file / 76 tests**
green (`d09-t4-fix-db.log`). Between them the seven cases prove that the column counts
`VARCHAR(n)` in characters rather than bytes — the behaviour the clamp is sized against — and
that a UTF-16-sliced value reaches the server as a substituted U+FFFD rather than an error. Whole-repo `pnpm format:check` fails at the base commit for 454 files nobody in this slice
touched (this worktree has `core.autocrlf=true` while Prettier wants LF); the files each task
touched were checked individually and are LF in the committed blobs.

**What is fixed, precisely.** Unset or blank, the API trusts nobody: a caller reaching the origin
directly is counted by the address it connected from and cannot rotate it by writing a header.
Where the operator names a proxy, only that peer's forwarded headers are believed.

**What is not, and is stated rather than left silent.**

- **A _misconfigured_ proxy still lets the client choose the address.** Where a proxy _is_
  configured, `request.ip` is the **right-most** `X-Forwarded-For` entry that is not itself
  trusted, taken **verbatim**: `@fastify/proxy-addr` builds `[socket peer, ...X-Forwarded-For
reversed]`, walks it while the entries are trusted, returns the first untrusted one, and never
  validates the element it returns. A proxy that **appends** its own observation therefore ends
  the walk on that observation — the client's entries sit to its left and are never reached — so
  **appending is the safe form**. Until this sweep every statement of this on the branch, the
  runbook included, said the opposite, and the runbook's nginx directive
  (`X-Forwarded-For $remote_addr`) would have collapsed every client behind a CDN into one
  address and applied `RATE_LIMIT_AUTH_MAX_PER_SOURCE` to the whole world at once. The three
  shapes that genuinely hand the address to the client — a proxy that forwards their header
  untouched, one that prepends its observation, and a trusted range broad enough to contain real
  clients — are now in `docs/runbooks/deploy.md` with the table they were measured from
  (`fastify@5.11.3`, inject and real sockets, `d09-fix-xff-probe.log`). Under any of them both
  address-keyed budgets rotate with the address. It remains a deployment fault with a deployment
  fix; what changed is which deployments have it.
- **D08 follow-up 6 stays open.** D09 makes the address _authentic_; it does not make it
  _scarce_. An IPv6 /64 still holds 2^64 addresses that rotate for free, so the source key can
  still be rotated by anybody who holds one, with no proxy involved. Canonicalising the address
  and keying IPv6 at /64 needs a slice of its own.
  - **Closed by x81 (2026-09-20).** `sourceComponent` in `sign-in-abuse-control.ts` now keys every IPv6 source on its canonical /64 network (IPv4-mapped `::ffff:a.b.c.d` as the IPv4 it carries, IPv4 unchanged, malformed input falling back to the clamped literal), so one /64 buys one source budget instead of 2^64; proved by unit cases, no DB test needed.
- **Not run:** e2e, the visual-regression baselines, the least-privilege suite, the rest of the
  `database` project, and the web typecheck. Nothing in the slice reaches a rendered surface.

**What was corrected in the sweep**, all of it prose: `sign-in-abuse-control.ts` and
`authentication.service.ts` (their header comments said the budgets were evadable by anyone who
could set a header, and that D09 was unfixed); `fastify-adapter.ts` (it said the forwarded
address behind a configured proxy was "the proxy's word and no longer anybody's", which
overstates it); `packages/config/src/env.ts` and `.env.example` (the `RATE_LIMIT_AUTH_MAX_GLOBAL`
rationale rested on `trustProxy: true`; the 3000 default survives it, because the spray it is
sized against is now paid for with authentic addresses rather than forged ones);
`.env.example` also gains `TRUSTED_PROXY_ADDRESSES` itself, which it had been missing since
`22a8072`; the doc comment on the D08 HTTP proxy case in `id-002-auth-http.db.test.ts` (its
`new FastifyAdapter()` with no trust is now the shipped default, not a divergence from
`main.ts`); and in this file, D08's follow-up 1, the "What this does not claim" bullet, the
ID-002 named gap 6, and the two ticket-accounting lines that listed D09 as the open P1.
Sentences that narrate a past state — the D08 fix-wave list, the probe records of earlier
sessions — were left exactly as they stand.

**What the whole-branch review then corrected**, also all prose, and the reason the sweep above
cannot be read as final. The reviewer measured `request.ip` against this branch's own
`fastify@5.11.3` and found the branch's central operator-facing caveat **backwards**: an
appending proxy is the safe shape, not the dangerous one, because its own observation is the
right-most entry and therefore the first untrusted one the walk reaches. The table was
re-measured here before anything was rewritten — six header shapes through `inject` with a
claimed peer of `203.0.113.7`, the same five again over real TCP sockets with a real peer, the
broad-range hazard, an untrusted peer, and the two-hop CDN case (`d09-fix-xff-probe.log`) — and
it reproduces exactly. Corrected: `docs/runbooks/deploy.md` (the caveat section replaced by the
mechanism, the measured table and the three real hazards; the nginx directive restored to
`$proxy_add_x_forwarded_for`, the Apache, Caddy and Traefik entries re-checked against the
vendors' own documentation, Traefik's append order marked **unverified**, and a second
post-deploy check added that distinguishes a pass-through or prepending proxy from a correct
one); `fastify-adapter.ts`, `sign-in-abuse-control.ts` (four places), `authentication.service.ts`
(two), `packages/config/src/env.ts`, `.env.example` (two), and the doc comments in
`id-002-auth-http.db.test.ts` and `sign-in-abuse-control.test.ts` — the last of which had also
called `request.ip` the _leftmost_ forwarded token. Where a comment reasoned _from_ the false
caveat to justify a clamp, the reasoning was rewritten and the clamp left standing: it is
justified by the three real hazards and by proxy-addr never validating the element it returns.
In this file: the head summary, the commit list, D08's follow-up 1 and named gap 6, the D09
"what is not" bullet, the clamp's stated reason, the case counts, and the engine assertions
listed under "Engine wording" below. No behaviour and no assertion was touched in either sweep.

**Engine wording.** Two present-tense assertions in this file that treated MariaDB as the
project's engine of record were corrected: the D07 "engine skew" item and the least-privilege
"not closed" note. MySQL is the only engine this project runs. Dated narration — the chain
records that say the DB suites "still ran on embedded MySQL 8.0, not MariaDB", and the
2026-08-13 spec-change table that records what the planning set said at the time — was left as
history. A separate branch is correcting engine claims across the repository and does not touch
this file.

**Ticket accounting.** A defect fixed on a branch, not a ticket: **35 of 70 tickets, 285 of 583
points (48.9%)** unchanged. D09, like D05 through D08 before it, is a review correction that
closes no ticket. D09 was the last P1 finding from the 2026-09-05 review still open after D08
merged; it is now **built and proved on a branch and waiting to be merged**, not merged. D08
follow-up 6 and the D11 dependency advisories are not P1 findings and are not closed by this
slice.

## D08 — the password endpoint had no source-based abuse control: built on a branch

**Finding** (production review of 2026-09-05, `CLAUDE-REVIEW-REPORT.md` §D08, P1), quoted as
the plan carried it:

> The installed request limiter is used on the binary upload-part parser. Password sign-in has
> per-user failure counting, but unknown accounts still incur hash verification and an
> authentication-event write, and rotating accounts avoids the user counter. This leaves
> credential spraying and CPU/log exhaustion uncontrolled at this boundary unless a verified
> edge control supplies the missing protection.
>
> **Fix:** add bounded source/global/account-aware controls before expensive hashing and
> writes, and test expected proxy behavior. Avoid turning one shared-office address into a
> permanent account lockout.
>
> **Acceptance:** a burst across unknown and distinct synthetic accounts is constrained before
> unbounded Argon2/log work; legitimate recovery and shared-IP traffic retain a reasonable path.

**What was built** (branch `d08-password-abuse-control`, cut from `master` `cb5afd7`; four
commits — `90cbe5f`, `ea2a33c`, `2c65fab`, `4036841`, the last of them the first fix wave — and
the later fix waves, one per bullet: `ce98302`, `9ceab73` and `7cc9c16` are committed, and the
final bullet is the fifth wave, which is in the working tree and which the orchestrator
commits).

**A note on the ordinals**, because two counts are in circulation and they differ. The commit
subjects and the fix-wave briefs number these waves without the `2b`: `9ceab73` calls itself
"fix wave 2b", `7cc9c16` calls itself "fix wave 3", and the brief behind the last bullet is
`fix-wave-4-findings.md`. This file has always counted `2b` as a wave in its own right, so from
the third onwards its ordinals run one ahead — `9ceab73` is the third here, `7cc9c16` the
fourth, and the wave the brief and the commit-subject scheme call "fix wave 4" is the fifth below. Neither count is
wrong; they count different things. Where a sentence could be read either way it names the
commit instead of an ordinal. What was built, then:

- `90cbe5f` — `apps/api/src/modules/identity/sign-in-abuse-control.ts`, an in-process control
  built from three fixed-window limiters and nothing else: no new dependency, no
  table, no Redis. The keys are consulted narrowest first and the first one that refuses ends
  the call, so the recorded reason is the tightest bound that fired. An **admitted** attempt
  charges all three; a **refused** attempt charges only the key that refused it — nothing wider
  and, since the two-phase charge of the fourth fix wave (`7cc9c16`), nothing narrower either
  (see the `ce98302` and `7cc9c16` bullets — charging every key on every attempt was a defect,
  in both directions). The one key a refusal does charge is the key that refused it, which is
  already over budget and moves no verdict.
  The account is hashed inside the module — SHA-256 from `node:crypto`, truncated to 16 hex
  characters — so the long-lived map holds buckets rather than a list of the addresses people
  typed. `packages/config` gained the three new tunables beside the existing one, `.env.example`
  carries all four, and `ApiConfig` exposes them as `authAbuse*`.
- `ea2a33c` — the control is consulted at the **top** of `signInWithPassword` (source,
  source+account and global), of `completeMfaChallenge` and `completeWithRecoveryCode` (source
  and global only — they are reached only with a signed challenge token, so the account key adds
  nothing) and of `confirmReauthentication` (D05), which is charged on all three keys exactly
  as password sign-in is — source, source+account and global — with the user id standing in for
  the email inside the hashed account key. A refused attempt reaches neither the user lookup nor
  the Argon2 verify, and writes at most the one bounded row described below.
  `identity.module.ts` builds the control from `ApiConfig`.
- `2c65fab` — this section, and the correction to ID-002 item 6.
- `4036841` — the **first fix wave** over the review of the branch: the discriminating
  precedence case, the whitespace-account case, three comment corrections, and the HTTP
  disclosure case hardened to read the `locked_out` row before comparing bodies.
- The **second fix wave**, over the final whole-branch review, and the reason several sentences
  above read differently from the plan. Three substantive changes, none of them cosmetic.
  **(1)** `admit()` now stops at the first refusal instead of charging every key on every
  attempt. Charging unconditionally meant one address could spend the deployment's entire global
  budget with attempts it was not being served — 601 requests in five minutes, about two a
  second, after which nobody could sign in until the window turned. The plan mandated the
  unconditional charge (PLAN.md:94, 173-178) and priced the global key only as protection, never
  as a denial lever; that is a hole in the plan, and this is the deliberate deviation from it.
  **(2)** `RATE_LIMIT_AUTH_MAX_GLOBAL` is **3000**, not 600, because the global key is a CPU
  bound for the deployment rather than an anomaly detector. **(3)** the source address is clamped
  to 45 characters before it is keyed, because wherever a proxy is trusted the address the key is
  built from is a forwarded token taken verbatim — text of any length rather than a validated
  address. The wave also corrects the false "the account key is not evadable that way" claim in
  all five places it was asserted, and adds five unit cases: the two halves of conditional
  charging, the clamp, the refusing-key eviction, and the limiter's own eviction caveat.
- The **third fix wave**, over the same final review's remaining findings. **(1)** The two
  enforcement points that had no test at any level now have one each: a database case per route
  spends a source budget with password posts and then proves that `POST /v1/auth/mfa` and
  `POST /v1/auth/recovery-code`, each carrying a valid challenge token, answer 429
  `rate_limited` with the password route's body byte for byte and add exactly one
  `authentication_events` row naming that route. **(2)** A failed audit write on a refusal path
  no longer turns the 429 into a 500: `record()` is wrapped there, the loss is reported on
  stderr, and the refusal is thrown regardless — the refusal is the control and the row is a
  trace of it, so the priority between them is now the right way round. **(3)** Three
  documentation corrections carrying no behaviour: the `sa:` key's normalisation is narrower
  than the column's collation and is therefore best-effort (see below), the source key is the
  literal address with no canonicalisation or IPv6 aggregation (follow-up 6), and `env.ts`
  states the multi-charge arithmetic behind the per-source default.
- The **fourth fix wave**, over the re-review of `4036841..9ceab73`. **(1)** The charge is now
  **two-phase**: `createTwoPhaseFixedWindowLimiter` (new in `rate-limiter.ts`, with
  `createFixedWindowLimiter` re-expressed in terms of it and unchanged from the outside) lets
  `admit()` ask all three budgets before spending any, so a refusal by a wider key no longer
  spends a narrower one. That is the other half of the wave-2 fix, and it is what makes "refused
  for the remainder of one window and never longer" true (re-review N-1). Two unit cases, both
  proved discriminating against the pre-fix module. **(2)** `countRecentFailures` excludes the
  three throttle reasons, so a `reauthentication` refusal can name a user without moving them
  towards their own durable lockout — before it, a colleague on the same address could lock
  somebody out with traffic that was never theirs (re-review N-2). One database case, proved
  discriminating against the pre-fix repository. **(3)** Corrections carrying no behaviour: the
  clamp constant's comment no longer claims the recorded row is truncated to match the key nor
  that a zoned IPv4-mapped address fits inside 45 characters; the lost-refusal-row log line
  carries a running loss count and the correlation id, because at one write per key per window a
  persistent failure is otherwise indistinguishable from a first one; `.env.example` records how
  much the global budget and the per-source arithmetic depend on D09 (what it says there has been
  rewritten twice since — by D09's own sweep, then by the whole-branch review that found the
  caveat backwards; today it says the address believed is the right-most `X-Forwarded-For` entry
  no trusted peer wrote, that an **appending** proxy is therefore the safe shape, and which three
  shapes are not); the per-source number is 15
  everywhere rather than "twelve to fifteen" in one place; and the unexecuted
  "deleting any one of the four `admit` calls fails a test" claim is reworded to what the
  evidence supports. `PLAN.md` (outside the repository, in the evidence directory) is amended in
  place with dated notes quoting each superseded clause.
- The **fifth fix wave**, over the four-lens review of `7cc9c16`. It is in the working tree as
  this paragraph is written and is **not yet committed**; the orchestrator commits it.
  **(1)** `countRecentFailures` no longer counts the `locked_out` row the lockout writes about
  itself. The three throttle reasons were excluded in the fourth wave; `locked_out` has exactly
  their shape — written in front of the password check, naming the victim, nothing read and
  nothing guessed — and was not excluded with them. While it was counted, every refusal pushed a
  fresh counted row into the very window the refusal was derived from, so the lockout renewed
  itself: at the shipped defaults (five failures in 900 s, ten requests per 300 s on the account
  key) roughly two attempts every five minutes held an account shut indefinitely — a third party
  who knows the address, or the victim's own retries, who are being told that waiting is the fix
  (A-1). The exclusion list is now the named constant `NON_CREDENTIAL_FAILURE_REASONS`, and the
  invariant it holds is that the count reads credentials that were presented and refused and
  never a row it caused itself. The audit trail is untouched again: the row is still written,
  still names the user and still carries `locked_out`; only the counter stopped reading it. One
  database case, proved discriminating against the pre-fix repository. **(2)** Three tests that
  asserted less than their titles claimed now assert it. The `reason IS NULL` half of that
  predicate — which no row this codebase writes reaches — is exercised by a row written through
  the repository (A-2); the charging-matrix case now spends a source budget the scenario can
  actually cross, so "neither narrower budget" is tested for the source key and not for the
  account key alone (A-3); and the lost-refusal-row log line is pinned by two refusals through
  one service instance, asserting the running loss count and each attempt's own correlation id
  (A-4). None of the three needed a production change. **(3)** Corrections carrying no
  behaviour, this paragraph among them: the two-phase charge and the throttle exclusion are
  credited to the fourth wave rather than the third, and the summary at the top of this file
  counts five waves rather than three; "the global key is charged only by admitted attempts" is
  corrected in all three places to the claim the module actually supports, that the global
  budget is only ever _crossed_ by admitted attempts; the N-2 comments say who writes a row that
  names a user (that user's own refused re-authentication — a third party supplies the refusal,
  not the row); the module's stale references to `createFixedWindowLimiter` and to the wrong
  section of this file are corrected; a database case's comment stops attributing a
  `source_account_throttled` row to traffic that cannot produce it; and the gate paragraphs
  below name the gate that ran after the database suites instead of claiming that none did.
  `PLAN.md` is amended in place once more, with a dated note quoting the superseded clause.

The three keys, asked in this order, and the first that is over budget refuses. An attempt that
all of them admit charges all of them; an attempt one of them refuses charges that key and no
other:

| key            | shape                                    | tunable                          | default | what it stops                              |
| -------------- | ---------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- | ------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| source+account | `sa:<ip>:<sha256(account) first 16 hex>` | `RATE_LIMIT_AUTH_MAX_REQUESTS`   | 4       | one address grinding one account           |
| source         | `s:<ip>`                                 | `RATE_LIMIT_AUTH_MAX_PER_SOURCE` | 30      | one address spraying many accounts         |
| global         | the constant `g`                         | `RATE_LIMIT_AUTH_MAX_GLOBAL`     | 3000    | a distributed spray from rotated addresses |

The source address is clamped to 45 characters — the width of `authentication_events.ip` —
before anything is keyed on it, so the keys are bounded in length as well as in count.

The window is `RATE_LIMIT_AUTH_WINDOW_SECONDS`, default **300** (five minutes).
`RATE_LIMIT_AUTH_MAX_REQUESTS` had existed since the limiter landed and was
consumed by nothing; D08 is what finally consumes it.

**The source+account budget is not free to choose (security audit 2026-09-12, C-1).** It shipped
at 10 against an `AUTH_MAX_FAILURES_IN_WINDOW` of 5, and ten is larger than five — so five wrong
passwords from one address sat inside the budget and drove any _known_ account into the
900-second lockout, renewably, for five requests a quarter-hour from one IP. Worse, the victim
could not clear it: `confirmReauthentication` reads the same `countRecentFailures` window and
re-authentication is the only gate to `setPassword`, so a locked-out person cannot change their
password to escape. The default is now **4**, and `packages/config` **refuses to boot** any
configuration where `RATE_LIMIT_AUTH_MAX_REQUESTS >= AUTH_MAX_FAILURES_IN_WINDOW`, naming both
variables. Bound on the shipped defaults by `packages/config/src/env.test.ts` and
`apps/api/src/common/http/api-config.test.ts` — deliberately not by literals of their own, which
is why `id-002-credentials.db.test.ts:677` passed throughout: it asserts the same inequality of
constants it declares itself.

**What that does not fix, stated plainly.** The two windows are different lengths — the budget is
per 300 s, the lockout counts over 900 s — so one address still gets 4 × 3 = 12 admitted failures
inside one lockout window, which is more than 5. Arming the lockout now costs a first window
instead of landing on the fifth request, and sustaining it is still possible. And the budget is
per address, not per account: the key is `sa:<ip>:<sha256(account)>`, so an attacker with any
address diversity — one IPv6 /64 is 2^64 keys — gets a fresh 4-request budget on each address and
reaches the fifth failure immediately, exactly as before this change. No value of the
budget closes that (the relation that would, `budget × ceil(900/300) < 5`, forces it to 1, which
refuses a real person their second try, and success is not exempt from the count). The durable
fix is the audit's own direction: stop letting a _wrong_ password deny a _right_ one — verify
first, and apply the durable window only to the failing path, so `locked_out` throttles guessing
instead of refusing the legitimate holder. That is a behaviour change in
`authentication.service.ts`, not a number, and is the next item.

**A refusal is not a lockout — with one exception, named below.** The fixed window self-heals: a
shared office is refused for the remainder of one five-minute window and never longer, and at the
**source and source+account keys** no account is locked by another party's traffic — those keys
refuse _requests from that source_, they do not touch the per-user failure counting in
`authentication_events`.

Both halves of that sentence are true only because of the **fourth** fix wave (`7cc9c16`), and
it is worth saying which defect each half closed.

- _"…and never longer."_ The decision is now **two-phase**: every applicable budget is asked,
  narrowest key first, before any of them is charged, and a refused attempt spends only the key
  that refused it. Until that landed, `sa:` was charged before `s:` was consulted, so a person
  behind a shared address burned their own account budget on attempts the source key refused —
  their `sa:` window started late, outlived the source window that had actually refused them,
  and left them throttled after their colleagues were signing in again (re-review N-1).
- _"…no account is locked by another party's traffic."_ `countRecentFailures` now excludes the
  three throttle reasons from the durable lockout count. Until it did, a `reauthentication`
  refusal under the per-source or global key — budgets everybody spends — wrote a `failed` row
  bearing the session holder's user id and counted towards `AUTH_MAX_FAILURES_IN_WINDOW` exactly
  as a wrong password did, so a colleague on the same office address could drive a named user
  into their own 900-second lockout (re-review N-2). The row naming the user is always written
  by that user's own re-authentication being refused; what the colleague supplies is the
  refusal, by keeping a budget everybody shares over its limit. The row is still written, still
  names the user and still carries its reason; only the counter stopped reading it.

One more window, and it is not the exception the paragraph above promises — that is the global
key, next. The **durable lockout has a window of its own, and until the fifth fix wave that
window did not end for as long as anyone kept knocking.** `countRecentFailures` excluded the
three throttle reasons but not `locked_out` — the row `signInWithPassword` writes against the
victim's own id when it finds the count already full. Every refusal therefore pushed a fresh
counted row into the very window the refusal was derived from, and at the shipped defaults (five
failures in 900 s, ten requests per 300 s on the account key) about two attempts every five
minutes held an account shut — a third party who knows the address, or the victim's own retries,
who are being told that waiting is the fix (A-1). The exclusion list is now
`NON_CREDENTIAL_FAILURE_REASONS` and the invariant is that the count reads credentials that were
presented and refused and never a
row it caused itself. The database case at `apps/api/test/id-002-credentials.db.test.ts` locks
an account, keeps attempting inside the window, asserts that the trail grows and the count does
not, and then lets the window pass and signs in
(`fix4-db-id-002-credentials.log`; `fix4-discrimination-probe-db.log` is the same suite against
the pre-fix repository, failing on that case).

The **global key is the exception**: a global admission bound is a global
refusal lever, and while its budget is spent every address and every account is refused until the
window turns. Two things make that a considered trade rather than a hole, and both are new in the
second fix wave. Its budget is **only ever crossed by admitted attempts** — not "charged only by"
them, which is what this sentence used to say and what the module's own header said beside a
paragraph contradicting it: a global refusal does charge the global key, on a budget already past
its limit, which moves no verdict. What a refused attempt never charges is a budget it did not
reach. So one address cannot take the global key over its limit — its own source key refuses it
thirty attempts in, and those refusals charge `s:` and nothing wider — and it is sized as a
**CPU bound rather than an anomaly detector**: 3000 per 300 s is about ten attempts a second, a fraction of what one core can
Argon2-verify, so it still stops a distributed spray from saturating the host while a single
attacker would have to sustain ten _admitted_ attempts a second to deny anybody else. The one
remaining route to it is address abundance — see "What this does not claim". The refusal is the 429 `rate_limited` the
per-user lockout already produced, byte-identical for a real and an unknown account because
nothing about the account has been looked up yet, and it writes **at most one**
`authentication_events` row per key per window, plus one more each time a key is evicted from
the module's refusing-key set once that set reaches `maxKeys` — the caveat the module's own
`createBudget` header states, and the price of bounding that set at all. The row carries
`outcome = 'failed'` and one of three new reasons — `source_throttled`,
`source_account_throttled`, `global_throttled` — which are never serialised to a caller. Its
`user_id` is `NULL` on the three `@Public()` routes, where nobody has been looked up yet; the
`confirmReauthentication` row names the real user, because the session guard established who
they are before the control was consulted — and since the fourth fix wave that row is _named_
without being _counted_: `countRecentFailures` excludes all three reasons (and, since the fifth,
the lockout's own `locked_out` row as well), so the trace an operator reads is intact and the
durable lockout no longer reads it. Success is counted as well as failure: a caller sitting
exactly at the boundary must not be able to keep guessing, which is why the per-source default
is 30 rather than 5.

**What this does not claim.**

- **It does not fix D09, and both address-keyed budgets rotate with the address.** This is the
  correction the final review's I1 asked for, because the branch previously claimed the opposite
  in five places. The source+account key is `sa:<ip>:<hash>` — it _contains_ the address — so
  rotating `X-Forwarded-For` rotates the source key **and** the source+account key together. It
  is not "not evadable that way". D08 shipped with that fully open: `main.ts` then set
  `trustProxy: true` unconditionally, so anyone who could set the header could rotate both keys
  at will, and the only bounds that held against them were the **global key** and the **durable
  per-user lockout** in `authentication_events` (`AUTH_MAX_FAILURES_IN_WINDOW`, 5 failures in
  900 s) — the lockout being the one that actually catches a grind against a named account,
  which is the honest reassurance. The trade ran both ways: that was also the one route by which
  an attacker could look like thousands of addresses and so spend the global budget with
  admitted attempts, which is the global refusal lever described above.

  **D09 has since closed the header half of this** (branch `d09-trusted-proxy`, see the D09
  section above). `main.ts` now passes `trustProxy: env.TRUSTED_PROXY_ADDRESSES`, unset means
  trust nobody, and a caller with no trusted proxy in front of them is counted by the socket
  peer. What is left of the paragraph above, and what the two address-keyed budgets are still
  worth, is stated there: a caller behind a **misconfigured** trusted proxy still chooses the
  address — a proxy that forwards their `X-Forwarded-For` untouched, one that prepends its own
  observation rather than appending it, or a trusted range broad enough to contain them — and
  address abundance (follow-up 6) is untouched by D09 for
  everybody. Both budgets therefore remain a cost bound on honest traffic rather than a control,
  and the global key and the lockout remain the bounds that hold.

  One HTTP case records the behaviour of an application built on a plain
  `new FastifyAdapter()` with no `trustProxy`, so a forged `x-forwarded-for` from the same
  socket buys nothing there. When it was written that harness diverged from the shipped API;
  since D09 it is the shipped **default**, and the request-level cases for both postures —
  nothing configured, and a configured proxy believed — are in
  `apps/api/src/common/http/trusted-proxy-requests.test.ts`.

- **The `sa:` account key is a best-effort narrowing, not a guarantee.** It hashes the account
  after `trim().toLowerCase()`, matching `findUserIdByEmail`; `users.email` is compared under
  `utf8mb4_unicode_ci` (`migrations/0001_tenancy.sql`), which is insensitive to accents and to
  compatibility variants as well as to case. So an accented or full-width variant of one real
  address resolves to the **same** user in the lookup and falls into a **different** bucket
  here, and a caller grinding one account can rotate the account key that way. The cost is
  bounded and the other three controls are untouched: the source key, the global key and the
  durable per-user lockout — which counts on the resolved `user_id` those variants share — all
  hold, so the degradation is from the account budget to the source budget, ten attempts a
  window to thirty at the defaults. Normalising harder (NFKD, strip combining marks) narrows
  the gap; closing it would mean keying on the resolved user id, which is the lookup this
  design exists to run after the decision rather than before it.
- **It does not survive a restart or a second API process.** The windows are process memory —
  the same trade `rate-limiter.ts` already documents, made legitimate by the same single API
  process `50-BOOTSTRAP` §3 assumes. A restart forgets every window, and if the deployment ever
  runs two API processes this control halves in strength and must move to the database.
- **It does not bound the total number of throttle event rows globally** — only one per key per
  window, plus one more per eviction from the refusing-key set. The global key's own refusal is
  the backstop for a rotating-address spray.
- **The per-source default of 30 has not been checked against the real deployment's topology.**
  Four routes charge that key, so one successful MFA sign-in charges it twice: 30 per five
  minutes is **fifteen** complete logins for _everything behind that address_ (30 ÷ 2 charges
  per MFA login), and a password change on top of one spends a third charge on
  `/v1/auth/reauth`. The number is 15 here, in `packages/config/src/env.ts` and in
  `.env.example`; an earlier "twelve to fifteen" in this file hedged an exact division.
  Behind an office NAT, or behind a fronting proxy that does not set `X-Forwarded-For`, that
  address may be the whole deployment. See follow-up 4.
- **`POST /v1/auth/password/set` (D06) is deliberately out of scope.** It runs an Argon2 _hash_,
  which costs more than a verify, but it requires both a live session and a fresh reauth token,
  and `confirmReauthentication` is now bounded in front of it.

**Follow-ups.**

1. **D09 (proxy headers trusted unconditionally) — ADDRESSED on branch `d09-trusted-proxy`.**
   As D08 left it: the worth of _both_ address-keyed budgets depended on it, because
   `sa:<ip>:<hash>` contains the address, so rotating `X-Forwarded-For` rotated the source and
   source+account keys together; both were to be read as advisory, with the global key and the
   durable per-user lockout as the ones that held. D08 also carried a second item into the
   slice: the same `request.ip` was inserted into `authentication_events.ip VARCHAR(45)` **with
   no truncation** (`credentials.repository.ts`, `recordAuthenticationEvent`), so under strict
   SQL mode a long forged header turned a failed sign-in into a 500. D08 clamped its own keys at
   45 characters and deliberately did not change that repository.

   Both are now done on `d09-trusted-proxy` (see the D09 section above). `main.ts` passes
   `trustProxy: env.TRUSTED_PROXY_ADDRESSES` and unset means trust nobody, so a host that can
   only reach the origin directly no longer presents as any number of addresses. And `0f779fb`
   clamps `ip` to 45 and `userAgent` to 255 by code point at the insert, so the sentence above
   about an untruncated insert is **no longer true**: an over-long value is truncated, the audit
   row survives, and the refusal stays a refusal instead of becoming a 500.

   **What the fix does not buy, and is not marked closed.** Where an operator does name a proxy,
   `request.ip` is the **right-most** untrusted `X-Forwarded-For` entry verbatim, so a client
   behind a _misconfigured_ proxy still chooses it: one that forwards their header untouched, one
   that prepends its own observation, or a trusted range wide enough to contain them. An
   _appending_ proxy is the safe shape, not one of those. The three, the measured table and the
   per-server directives are in `docs/runbooks/deploy.md`. And part of the source key's weakness
   **outlives D09 and stays open as follow-up 6**: D09 made the address _authentic_, it did not
   make it _scarce_, and an IPv6 /64 still holds 2^64 addresses that rotate for free. Raising
   the global default to 3000 remains what raises the cost of a spray; nothing here removes it.

2. **If a second API process is ever run**, this control must move to the database or another
   shared store. In-process state is only legitimate while `50-BOOTSTRAP` §3's single API
   process holds, and a restart forgets every window in the meantime.
3. **The throttle row bound is per key per window, not global** — and not flat even at that:
   the set of currently refusing keys is itself capped at `maxKeys`, and each eviction from it
   costs one extra row for the evicted key in that window, as `createBudget`'s own header says.
   A spray from rotated addresses can still write one row per new source key until the global
   key refuses; that refusal is the only thing that caps the total.
4. **Confirm the deployment's `request.ip` topology before relying on the per-source default.**
   One log line on the real host is enough: does `request.ip` vary per client, or is it one
   address for everybody? If the deployment sits behind a NAT of any size, or behind a fronting
   proxy that does not set `X-Forwarded-For`, raise `RATE_LIMIT_AUTH_MAX_PER_SOURCE`
   deliberately and record why — 30 charges per address per five minutes is fifteen complete
   MFA logins for everything behind that address (two charges each), and morning login traffic
   crosses it in the first window. A candidate refinement, deliberately not taken in this
   branch because it changes which call sites charge which key: do **not** charge the source key
   for the MFA or recovery-code _completion_ of a challenge the same source already paid for at
   the password step — the challenge token is signed, so that step is not the spray surface the
   finding names.
5. **`global_throttled` is still asserted at unit level only.** The MFA and recovery-code call
   sites were the other half of this gap and the third fix wave closed them, with one HTTP case
   each. No database or HTTP case produces a `global_throttled` row, because reaching the global
   key over HTTP means admitting thousands of attempts from distinct addresses in one suite;
   the module-level case is what stands behind that reason and the row's shape is the same
   `record()` call the other two reasons prove.
6. **Canonicalise the source address, and key IPv6 at /64.** The key is the address string
   verbatim (trimmed and clamped), so `2001:DB8::1`, `2001:db8::1`, `::ffff:203.0.113.9` and
   `203.0.113.9` are four keys for what may be one or two hosts — and a caller on a single
   IPv6 /64 holds 2^64 of them and can rotate for free. This was **not** cured by D09, and is
   **still open**: proxy trust decides whether the address is authentic, not whether it is
   scarce. It was expected to be done in the same slice as D09, since both touch how
   `request.ip` is read; D09 deliberately did not take it, so it needs a slice of its own.

**Ticket accounting.** A defect fixed on a branch, not a ticket: **35 of 70 tickets, 285 of 583
points (48.9%)** unchanged. D08, like D05, W01, W02, D06 and D07 before it, is a review

## D07 — TOTP seeds stored as recoverable plaintext: fixed, proved, merged

**Finding** (production review of 2026-09-05, `CLAUDE-REVIEW-REPORT.md` §D07, P1), quoted as
the plan carried it:

> The base32 seed is passed directly to the secret column
> (`apps/api/migrations/0004_credentials.sql:97`, `credentials.repository.ts:163`,
> `authentication.service.ts:522`). TOTP does require a recoverable secret, but that does not
> require plaintext storage. A database read or backup disclosure would expose the second-factor
> seeds. The worker's database-wide SELECT grant also unnecessarily includes credential tables.
>
> **Fix:** encrypt MFA seeds with authenticated encryption and a versioned key outside the
> database; scope decryption to identity processing; design rotation/backfill and recovery.
> Reduce worker read privileges to its real table dependencies.
>
> **Acceptance:** a database dump contains ciphertext rather than usable seeds; altered
> ciphertext is rejected; rotation works; the worker credential cannot read password/MFA/recovery
> tables.

**What was built** (branch `d07-totp-seed-encryption`, cut from `master` `2a15603`; five commits
plus a merge of `master` `282f243` back into the branch at `5c94de4`):

- `72c3738` — the cipher and the key format. `packages/config/src/seed-keys.ts` holds the single
  parser, `parseSeedKeys`, for a new **required** environment variable `AUTH_MFA_SEED_KEYS`:
  entries `<version>:<base64url 32-byte key>` separated by `;`, the **highest** version is the
  active one and every other entry is decrypt-only. It refuses rather than repairs (empty list,
  missing `:`, non-positive-integer version, duplicate version, a key outside the base64url
  alphabet, a key that does not decode to exactly 32 bytes), and it checks the alphabet _before_
  decoding, because Node's base64 decoder silently drops stray characters and a key pasted in
  standard base64 would otherwise become a different 32-byte key with no complaint.
  `apps/api/src/modules/identity/seed-cipher.ts` builds AES-256-GCM `encrypt` / `decrypt` /
  `keyVersionOf` / `needsRotation` on `node:crypto` alone — no new dependency. `packages/config`
  validates the variable at boot with the same parser, `.env.example` carries a
  `local_dev_only` key that production refuses, and the parsed keyring reaches the API as
  `config.mfaSeedKeys`.
- **The stored envelope** is one string in the existing `user_mfa_factors.secret` column:
  `mfa1.<version>.<iv>.<ciphertext>.<tag>`, all base64url, a fresh random 12-byte IV per
  encryption and a 16-byte tag. The **additional authenticated data is the owning `user_id`**,
  so a ciphertext copied into somebody else's row fails to authenticate. Anything that does not
  begin with `mfa1.` is not a valid stored seed: it is refused at read time with an error naming
  the backfill command, never quietly used.
- `ec32140` — the worker's one database-wide `GRANT SELECT` over the whole `tmanage` schema is
  replaced by **fourteen table-level SELECT grants** in `scripts/db/users.sql`, grouped and
  commented by the subsystem that reads them. As originally written the replacement held only for
  **accounts created by the script from then on**: the file performed no `REVOKE` and created the
  user with `CREATE USER IF NOT EXISTS`, so an account provisioned under the previous script kept
  its database-wide SELECT when `db:grants` was re-applied, and `users-sql.test.ts` could not see
  it because it asserts the _script's_ grants (`code-review-2026-09-12/REVIEW.md` R10, P1). Every
  other worker grant is unchanged, and `tmanage_app` is deliberately left alone (its own tests
  still depend on its database-wide SELECT). `users-sql.test.ts` gained assertions that the worker
  never receives a database-wide SELECT and is never granted anything on `user_passwords`,
  `user_mfa_factors`, `user_recovery_codes` or `authentication_events`, and
  `least-privilege.db.test.ts` gained a live worker-credential case.
  **Closed on branch `x13-grant-revokes` (not merged):** the script now issues
  `REVOKE ALL PRIVILEGES, GRANT OPTION` against each of `tmanage_app`, `tmanage_worker` and
  `tmanage_migrator`, between that principal's `CREATE USER` and its first `GRANT`, and enumerates
  each principal's intended privilege set in the file itself, so `pnpm db:grants` is corrective as
  well as additive and idempotent in the strong sense. The upgrade path is proved statically by
  `apps/api/src/common/database/grants.test.ts` and `users-sql.test.ts` (executed); the check that
  reads the privileges **actually in force** on a server and fails on any excess is
  `apps/api/test/grant-reconciliation.db.test.ts`, which is **written and not executed** — it needs
  `TMANAGE_TEST_GRANT_ADMIN_DATABASE_URL` pointed at a provisioned server, and this machine's
  database suite runs as an administrative user, where a missing grant is invisible.
- `e45f47c` — the repository became the encryption boundary.
  `CredentialsRepository` takes the cipher in its constructor with no default, `createFactor`
  encrypts, and every read path that hands a seed upward decrypts using **the row's own
  `user_id`** as the AAD rather than an id the caller passed. Nothing above the repository
  changed: the service, `totp.ts`, `challenge-token.ts` and the controller still see the same
  base32 seed they always did. Backfill and rotation live in
  `apps/api/src/modules/identity/seed-backfill.repository.ts` and are driven from
  `apps/api/src/common/database/cli.ts` as `mfa-seeds encrypt` and `mfa-seeds status`, with the
  package scripts `mfa:encrypt-seeds` and `mfa:seeds-status`. The sweep reads every row once and
  then writes one row at a time with the previous value in the `WHERE` clause, so a concurrent
  enrolment is reported rather than clobbered, and a row it cannot open is counted and left
  exactly as it is — re-encrypting a tampered row would replace the evidence with something that
  looks correct.
- `b5fce8b` — first review wave. Listing and removing a factor no longer decrypt anything: the
  listing selects four named columns into its own summary type, and removal goes through a new
  `findFactorIdentity` that reads only the id and the owner. So somebody whose seed cannot be
  opened can still see the factor on their security screen and delete it.
- `de22781` — second review wave. `listActiveFactors` now **partitions**: it returns the factors
  that open and throws only when rows existed and none of them opened, so a person holding two
  authenticators is no longer locked out by one broken row, while a person whose only row is
  broken still fails closed (skipping unopenable rows unconditionally would be an MFA bypass for
  anyone who could write one column). `mfa:seeds-status` now reports an `unopenable` count with
  the offending factor ids. And `docs/runbooks/deploy.md` was written — at exactly the path
  `scripts/db/users.sql` already pointed at — covering the deploy order, key generation and
  custody, rotation, and operator recovery for a row that will not open.

**Deployment order, which this change makes mandatory.** `AUTH_MFA_SEED_KEYS` must be set for
every process before the deploy — the API, the worker, `verify` and `sweep` all refuse to boot
without it, although only the API decrypts anything — and
`pnpm --filter @tmanage/api mfa:encrypt-seeds` must be run **immediately** after the deploy.
Between the two, every pre-existing MFA row is still bare base32, so every MFA user's sign-in
fails, and the error text is discarded before it reaches a screen. All of this, including where
the key is held and what to do with a row that still will not open, is in
`docs/runbooks/deploy.md`.

**Evidence** (`C:/Users/Peter/Documents/ChatGPT/TManage/d07-totp-seed-encryption-2026-09-06/`).
Every claim below names the command and the log.

- Unit and static gates at `de22781`: `pnpm --filter @tmanage/api typecheck`,
  `pnpm --filter @tmanage/web typecheck` and `pnpm --filter @tmanage/e2e typecheck` all clean

- **Least privilege, actually executed** (`lp-proof.md`): `least-privilege.db.test.ts` ran **34
