## D06 — replacing a password left every other session alive: fixed, proved, merged

**Finding** (Codex review of 2026-09-05, `CLAUDE-REVIEW-REPORT.md` lines 134–141, P1):
`AuthenticationService.setPassword` wrote the new hash and an authentication event and
nothing else, so a person replacing their password to recover from a suspected compromise
left every session the intruder already held alive, access and refresh alike. Confirmed at
`8c59cc6` by reading `setPassword` (no call to any revocation) and `SessionService`, whose
`revokeAllForUser` existed and was called by nobody.

**Policy chosen** (Peter delegated the open decisions on 2026-09-05): replacing a password ends
**every other live session** of the person, in the **same transaction** as the new hash, with
`sessions.revoked_reason = 'password_changed'`. The session that carried the change is kept — it
is the device in the person's hand, and `D05` already bound the proof to it, which is the
fresh proof the finding asks for before a session survives. Refresh credentials end with the
session row, because `SessionService.refresh` and `authenticate` both refuse a revoked
session; nothing separate is needed for them. A **first** password ends nothing: no session
was ever opened against a password that is now stale. A refused or rejected replacement (no
proof, weak password) ends nothing either — the cutoff lands with the hash or not at all.

**What was built** (branch `d06-password-session-cutoff`, commit `87fc4fd`, rebased on
`8c59cc6`):

- `SessionsRepository.revokeOthersForUser(runner, userId, keepSessionId, reason)` — the
  `revokeAllForUser` statement with one `id <> keep` predicate added; live rows only.
- `AuthenticationService` takes a `SessionsRepository` as a fifth constructor argument
  (stateless, so the default is the real one and `identity.module.ts` is unchanged) and
  exports `PASSWORD_CHANGE_REVOCATION_REASON`. `setPassword` reads whether a password already
  exists (it did for `D05`), and when it does the transaction declares `sessions` as well as the
  identity tables and revokes the others between writing the hash and recording the event.
- No web change: no screen calls `setPassword` yet (recorded under D05), so the user-facing
  explanation the finding asks for belongs to the first screen that does. Recorded as open.

**Evidence** (`C:/Users/Peter/Documents/ChatGPT/TManage/d06-password-cutoff-2026-09-06/`):
`pnpm typecheck` for `@tmanage/api` and `@tmanage/web` clean (the first web run failed only
because the worktree's built `@tmanage/config` predated W02; `pnpm build:packages` fixed it);
eslint and prettier on the four touched files clean; `@tmanage/api` unit project **24 files,
337 tests, all pass**; `id-002-credentials.db.test.ts` + `id-002-auth-http.db.test.ts` +
`sessions.db.test.ts` on the local database under `locks/db-e2e.lock`, **3 files, 122 tests,
all pass** (`db-identity-run.log`) — three new service-level cases under `D06 — replacing a
password ends every other session` (revokes the others with the reason and keeps the proving
one, and never touches another person's sessions; ends nothing on a first password; ends
nothing on a refused or rejected replacement) and one HTTP acceptance case exactly as the
review states it (two devices, the other one answers 401 on the device list and on refresh
immediately, the device in hand still refreshes and lists one session). Reverse proof by file
copy, never `git checkout`: with the `HEAD` service and repository swapped back in and the new
tests kept, **the two revocation cases fail and the two "ends nothing" guards pass**
(`reverse-run.log`, 2 failed / 77 passed); the corrected bytes restored by copy re-pass
(`restore-run.log`, 79/79), SHA-256 verified before and after (`hashes-corrected.txt`,
`hashes-reverse-state.txt`, `hashes-after-restore.txt`).

**Ticket accounting.** A defect closed, not a ticket: **35 of 70 tickets, 285 of 583 points
(48.9%)** unchanged. Re-derived this run against the sections below: FILE-002 (13 points,
slices A–C) closed on 2026-09-05; D05, W01, W02 and D06 are review corrections that close no
ticket. **D07** (TOTP seeds in plaintext) has since been fixed and proved on the branch
`d07-totp-seed-encryption` and is waiting to be merged — see the D07 section above. Remaining P1

## D05 — password, second factor and recovery codes could be replaced by any live session: built on a branch

**Finding** (Codex review of 2026-09-05, `CLAUDE-REVIEW-REPORT.md` lines 125–132, P1):
`POST /v1/auth/password/set`, `DELETE /v1/auth/factors/:factorId` and
`POST /v1/auth/recovery-codes` required only an ordinary session. A hijacked or left-open
session could replace the password, remove the second factor, or reissue the recovery codes
and keep the account after its owner noticed. Confirmed at `1d89a04` by reading
`CredentialsController` and `AuthenticationService`: none of the three read a password, a
code or any fresher proof than the session cookie.

**What was built** (worktree `tmanage-d05`, branch `d05-reauth`, no commit):

- `apps/api/src/modules/identity/reauth-token.ts` — a signed, stateless, five-minute token
  in the shape of `challenge-token.ts`, with its own purpose string (`reauth`) so a challenge
  token is refused as `malformed` before any signature is compared, and with the
  **session id inside the signed claims**. Unit-tested in `reauth-token.test.ts` (16 cases).
- `AuthenticationService.confirmReauthentication` — re-verifies the password with the
  sign-in discipline (shared per-user lockout window, dummy-hash verify when no password
  exists, one coarse `invalid_credentials` for every cause); if a confirmed factor exists a
  TOTP code is required and spent through the same replay-protected loop `ID-02` uses,
  which was extracted into a private `spendTotpCode` helper rather than duplicated. Mints a
  token bound to `userId` + `sessionId`. Every attempt is a `reauthentication` row in
  `authentication_events`.
- `requireReauth` (private) — verifies the token and separately checks that its claims name
  the caller's own user **and** session. Refusals throw the new
  `ReauthenticationRequiredError` with a precise reason (`reauth_required`, `reauth_invalid`,
  `reauth_expired`, `reauth_wrong_session`) that goes to the log only.
- Enforcement: `setPassword` demands proof only when a password row **already exists**, so a
  first-ever password (the invited person's enrolment) still goes through with no token;
  `disableFactor` and `regenerateRecoveryCodes` always demand it, because the state they act
  on only exists after enrolment. Each now takes `sessionId` and an optional `reauthToken`.
- HTTP: new `POST /v1/auth/reauth` on `CredentialsController` (session required, `@NoTenant`,
  body `{ password, code? }`, returns `{ reauthToken, expiresAt }`, refuses with the same 401
  body a wrong sign-in gets and 429 when locked out). The three guarded routes read the
  `x-reauth-token` header and answer **403 `reauthentication_required`** without it — a new
  `ApiErrorCode` in the API and mirrored by hand in `apps/web/src/lib/api/errors.ts`, per
  that file's own note. The session stays usable after a refusal.

**Evidence** (`C:/Users/Peter/Documents/ChatGPT/TManage/d05-implementation-2026-09-06/`):
`pnpm typecheck` for `@tmanage/api` and `@tmanage/web` clean; eslint on the eight touched
files clean; prettier clean after LF normalisation; `@tmanage/api` unit project **22 files,
328 tests, all pass**; `id-002-credentials.db.test.ts` + `id-002-auth-http.db.test.ts` on the
local database started by `mysql-memory-server` — **MySQL**, per the machine table below and the
correction in `c61f7ea` — serialised under `locks/db-e2e.lock`, **2 files, 75 tests, all pass** (12 new
service-level cases under `D05 — re-authentication before a credential changes`, 6 new HTTP
cases under `re-authentication over HTTP`, and the pre-existing cases re-threaded with a
session id and proof). Reverse proof by file copy, never `git checkout`: with the `HEAD`
service and controller swapped back in, the same two suites fail on the D05 cases; the
corrected bytes restored by copy re-pass, SHA-256 verified before and after
(`hashes-corrected.txt`, `hashes-reverse-state.txt`, `hashes-after-restore.txt`,
`reverse-run.log`, `restore-run.log`, `api-unit-final.log`).

**Deferred, recorded as open gaps rather than dropped:**

- _Notify the account owner of changes_ — the review's secondary hardening. No generic
  security-notification mailer exists; building one means new DI wiring in
  `identity.module.ts`, a second `Mailer` consumer beside `InvitationMailer`, and templates.
  Real scope of its own; not started.
- ~~`confirmTotpEnrolment` (adding a further factor while one is confirmed) is outside the
  review's cited lines and was left as it was.~~ **This was the hole, and the sentence
  understated it.** Confirming a factor calls `replaceRecoveryCodes` and returns the new set,
  so leaving it ungated left the destruction and disclosure of recovery credentials reachable
  from a live session — the very thing D05 exists to prevent — whether or not a factor was
  already confirmed. Closed 2026-09-12; see **D05c** below.
- The web client helpers `setPassword`, `disableFactor` and `regenerateRecoveryCodes` in
  `apps/web/src/lib/api/auth.ts` do not yet send the header and there is no `reauthenticate`
  helper; nothing in `apps/web/src` calls them today, so no screen regressed, but the first
  screen to use them needs the header and a password prompt on `reauthentication_required`.
- Acceptance, integration onto `master` and the full chain remain Codex's (the parallel
  arrangement of 2026-09-05); this slice ran the two identity DB suites, not `pnpm test:db`.

## D05c — TOTP enrolment could still destroy and reveal the recovery codes: fixed on a branch

**Finding** (re-review of 2026-09-12). D05's third clause was never enforced.
`POST /v1/auth/factors/totp` and `POST /v1/auth/factors/totp/confirm` called neither
`reauthTokenOf` nor anything equivalent, and `AuthenticationService.confirmTotpFactor` carried
no `requireReauth`. Confirming a factor calls `CredentialsRepository.replaceRecoveryCodes` and
returns the new set to the caller — which is precisely what `regenerateRecoveryCodes` does and
has been gated for since D05.

**What an attacker with only a live session could do.** Holding a stolen or fixated cookie, a
session left open on a shared machine, an unattended browser: post to `/v1/auth/factors/totp`,
post the code back to `/confirm`, and walk away with a fresh set of recovery codes. The
account owner's own codes — the ones written down at enrolment — stopped working at that
moment, and the codes that did work were the attacker's. No password was ever presented. The
record made this harder to see twice over: the D05 deferral described it as "adding a further
factor while one is confirmed", which understates it, and the D08 accounting then listed D09
as the only remaining P1. Both sentences are corrected above.

**The fix.** `beginTotpEnrolment` and `confirmTotpFactor` each take `sessionId` and an
optional `reauthToken` and open with the existing `requireReauth`, in the same shape as
`disableFactor` and `regenerateRecoveryCodes` — no second mechanism was invented. Both
controller routes read `x-reauth-token` through `reauthTokenOf`, pass the full
`contextOf(...)` so the refusal row carries an address, and map the refusal through the
existing `translateReauth` to **403 `reauthentication_required`**. The happy path is
unchanged.

**Which of the two carries the gate, and why both do.** The gate that _has_ to exist is on
`confirmTotpFactor`: that is the method which reaches `replaceRecoveryCodes`, and a gate on
`beginTotpEnrolment` alone would close nothing, because a caller can post straight to
`/confirm` with an id it already holds. The gate on `beginTotpEnrolment` is the second half of
the pair and earns its place twice: it refuses before a pending factor row is written, and
before an account-bound TOTP seed is generated and returned to a caller who has shown nothing
but a cookie. It also fails at a point a person can act on — the password is asked for before
the QR code rather than after it has been scanned. Both are checked **before** the ownership
lookup, so the refusal for a missing token does not differ between a real factor id and an
invented one. There is no first-password exemption of the kind `setPassword` has: an account
with no password cannot re-authenticate, but that is already true of `disableFactor` and
`regenerateRecoveryCodes`, and a second factor guarding an account with no first one guards
nothing.

**Tests, written before the fix.**

- `id-002-auth-http.db.test.ts`, under `re-authentication over HTTP`: with a live session and
  no proof, both routes answer 403, no factor row appears, the stored `code_hash` set is
  unchanged, and — the assertion that matters — the owner's own recovery code still completes
  a sign-in afterwards. A second case runs the enrolment end to end with the proof presented
  and shows the new set replacing the old one.
- `authentication.enrolment-reauth.test.ts` (new, unit): the service against a repository that
  fails the case if `createFactor`, `findFactor` or `replaceRecoveryCodes` is reached at all.
  That is a statement about _order_ the HTTP suite cannot make — a gate placed after the
  ownership lookup would answer 403 and still be wrong.
- No existing assertion was weakened or deleted. Four existing call sites reached the
  enrolment routes without proof as a _precondition_ (the `enrol()` helper, the factor-listing
  case, the someone-else's-factor 404, and the D05 remove-and-reissue case) and were rethreaded
  with a token; the service-level suite's enrolment helpers took `sessionId` and a minted
  token the same way D05 rethreaded the rest.

**Evidence** (`C:/Users/Peter/Documents/ChatGPT/TManage/d05c-recovery-reauth-2026-09-12/`):
probe logs from before the fix (`probe-unit-before-fix.log`, `probe-db-before-fix.log`),
`typecheck-api.log`, `test-api-unit.log`, `test-db-identity.log`, `lint.log`, prettier on the
touched files, and the reverse proof by file copy with SHA-256 verified before and after
(`pre-fix-hashes.txt`, `post-fix-hashes.txt`, `reverse-*.log`, `hashes-after-restore.txt`).
The database engine is MySQL, started by `mysql-memory-server`.

**Left alone, deliberately:** the web client helpers in `apps/web/src/lib/api/auth.ts` send no
`x-reauth-token` for _any_ gated route — not for `setPassword`, `disableFactor` or
`regenerateRecoveryCodes` either — and nothing in `apps/web/src` calls them yet. The two
enrolment helpers now sit in exactly the same position as the other three, so the first screen
to use any of them needs the header and a password prompt on `reauthentication_required`, as
D05 already recorded. Adding the header to two of the five and not the others would have been
a second convention.

## W01 — the scan pass could wait forever after a source or sink failure: fixed on a branch

**Finding** (Codex review of 2026-09-05, `CLAUDE-REVIEW-REPORT.md` §5, P1; reviewed revision
`af27739`, re-probed on `7b95864`): in `FileScanner.judge`, the inner catch awaited the
scanner's settlement **before** the tee into the scanner (`toScanner`, a `PassThrough`) was
ended or destroyed. Every driver drains its stream to the end by contract, so after a read or
sink failure the pass waited for an end it could no longer send. **Confirmed** at `1d89a04`:
the same tee stalls the other way too — an engine that fails early stops reading, and the
pass's next write into the full `PassThrough` never calls back. A third hazard surfaced while
writing the witness: a sink that fails a write also emits `error`, and nobody listened, so a
failing promotion sink would have taken the process down rather than the asset.

**Fix** (`apps/api/src/modules/files/file-scanner.ts`, `judge` only): the engine's settlement
is watched from the moment it starts, and once it has settled with the tee still open the
tee is destroyed so a pending write fails instead of waiting; in the catch, both streams are
destroyed **before** the engine is awaited; whether the engine broke on its own is read before
it is released, so a failure it reports only because it was cut off does not rewrite the
primary cause (`size_mismatch` stays `size_mismatch`); the promotion abort is best-effort
and separately observable (`abortQuietly`: one stderr line, the cause preserved, an
unavailable store still stops the pass); the sink's `error` event is heard. The happy path,
the infected path and the verdict precedence rule are unchanged.

**Witness** (`apps/api/src/modules/files/file-scanner.test.ts`, the `unit` project, no
database): source failure, sink failure, early engine failure and a mid-loop size mismatch
each raced against a 1 s clock, plus the happy path. Pre-fix source (SHA-256
`44071717aa5a…565a80`, the committed file at `1d89a04`): **4 of 5 fail**, each `still pending`
at 1 s, and the sink case raises an uncaught exception. Fixed source (`5bd3eb7df06d…5abb0`):
**5 of 5 pass in 20 ms**; restored by copy and re-run, 5 of 5. Codex's own probe
(`review-probes.mts`, root pointed at the branch's worktree) now reports `after350ms:
"rejected"` and `cleanupReachedBeforeIntervention: true`. On the branch: prettier, eslint and
the api typecheck pass; the api `unit` project is 22 files, 315 tests; the FILE-002 scanning
database suite result is recorded in the parallel-desk `result.md`.

**Not done here, on purpose:** a whole-operation timeout for a _source_ stream that stalls
without failing. The ClamAV driver bounds an engine stall with `MALWARE_SCAN_TIMEOUT_MS`; a
quarantine read that hangs is the store's to bound, and the local store does not hang. It is
an open risk on the pass, not a regression of this fix, and is carried.

**Where it lives:** branch `w01-scanner-cleanup`, worktree `tmanage-w01`, cut from `1d89a04`.
Not committed to `master` and not pushed: the parallel arrangement of 2026-09-05 makes Codex
the reviewer and default integrator, and the brief says the proposed fix is not landed before
that review. The diff, the proof logs and the probe output are under
`C:/Users/Peter/Documents/ChatGPT/TManage/w01-proof/`. No ticket closes: **35/70, 285/583
points (48.9%)**; W01 is a repair inside FILE-002, which stays closed.

**Other review probes at `1d89a04`, same run, unchanged:** D01 (sign-out keeps another user's
cached organizations and work), D02 (browser reads `tm_session_csrf`, server default
`tmanage_session_csrf`), conditional D09 (two forwarded addresses on one socket both admitted),

## W01 correction — a blocked write into the destroyed tee never called back (Codex re-review of 2026-09-06)

**Finding** (`CODEX-W01-REVIEW-2026-09-06.md`, P1; reviewed revision `1d89a04`, the W01 fix
above): the settlement handler destroyed `toScanner` with a plain `.destroy()` and no error.
On Node 22.22.0, when a write into that `PassThrough` was already blocked behind the readable
side's high-water mark (nobody was draining it — an engine that answered only after it had
stopped reading), destroying the stream did not reliably invoke that write's own callback.
`writeTo` only listened on the callback, so `judge` never re-entered its catch, never
destroyed the source or aborted the promotion, and a scan that already had a known engine
failure could not conclude. Distinct from the four W01 paths already proved: those all
resolved or rejected a write that had not yet started blocking.

**Fix** (`file-scanner.ts`, `writeTo` only): the promise now also races the sink's own
`close` event — always emitted once, whatever destroyed it and whether or not the write
callback fires — and its `error` event, each guarded so only the first settlement wins and
listeners are removed either way. Nothing else in `judge` changed; the precedence logic
that keeps the engine's own cause when it broke first (`engineBrokeFirst`) is what actually
turns this unblock into the right `ScanFailure`, unchanged from the fix above.

**Witness** (new test in `file-scanner.test.ts`, `unit` project, no database): a 64 KiB
source into an engine that never reads and rejects with `ScanError('engine_error')` only
after 50 ms — long enough for a write to be genuinely stuck, not merely about to start.
Reviewed bytes (SHA-256 `5bd3eb7d…4b5abb0`): 5 of 6 pass, the new witness `still pending` at
1,041 ms. Corrected bytes (`6c856d76…50404a`): 6 of 6 pass in 70–80 ms. Reverted to the
reviewed copy by file copy (never `git checkout`) and re-run: the same single failure
reproduces exactly; restored to the corrected copy and re-run: 6 of 6 pass again. Full
`pnpm --filter @tmanage/api build` then `pnpm test:unit`: 22 files, 316 tests, all pass. The
scoped `test/file-002-scanning.db.test.ts` (`database` project, real MariaDB, serialized
under `locks/db-e2e.lock`): 15 of 15 pass, 89 s. Evidence, logs and both file copies are under
`C:/Users/Peter/Documents/ChatGPT/TManage/w01-correction-2026-09-06/`.

**Not re-opened here:** the disclosed unbounded source-stall risk (a quarantine read that
hangs without failing) remains an open, separately carried risk, not part of this P1.

**Where it lives:** the same branch as the W01 fix above, **since committed, merged into `master`
and pushed**. The `awaiting_codex_review` handoff recorded here (via `cycle-state.json`, `claude`
lane, run `claude-w01-1788701585`) belonged to the parallel arrangement that ended 2026-09-06
17:44; no Codex review gate exists.

## D20 and the D19 build witness — the session/browser slice continued on the same branch

Codex's status file was unchanged (2026-09-05 22:58) when this session began, so neither branch
was landed; the work below continues `w02-session-browser` exactly as the previous entry's
"not done here" list and the handoff prescribed. Nothing on `master` was touched.

**D20 — the API's CORS policy never allowed `DELETE`.** Confirmed at `1d89a04` by the D01
journey's trace (previous entry) and now by a unit witness. The cause is more specific than the
previous entry said: `@fastify/cors` 11.3.0 — the plugin `@nestjs/platform-fastify` registers —
defaults `methods` to **`GET,HEAD,POST`**, not the `cors` package's six, so `PUT` and `PATCH`
were refused cross-origin as well as `DELETE` (the browser sends a `PATCH` for a work-item
edit and would send `PUT` for an upload part). Changed: `apps/api/src/common/http/cors.ts`
(new) holds the policy as one value — the origin list, credentials, the six methods, the
allowed and exposed headers, with the reasons — and `main.ts` passes `corsOptions(...)` to
`enableCors`; the inline object and its comment moved there so a test can reach it. Witness:
`cors.test.ts` (3) — a minimal Nest/Fastify application with the same options answers a
preflight for `DELETE` carrying `x-csrf-token` from an allowed origin with `204`, the origin
echoed, credentials allowed, `DELETE` in `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`; the same for `PUT`
and `PATCH`; a stranger origin is not named. **Reversal** (`w02-proof/d20/`): `cors.ts` swapped
for a copy without the `methods` line (SHA `e64ac36c…`), **2 of 3 fail** — `expected [ 'GET',
'HEAD', 'POST' ] to include 'DELETE'` — restored by copy, SHA re-verified (`6c5d584f…`), **3 of
3**. The api `unit` project: 22 files, **313 tests** (was 310). The api typecheck (after
`build:worker`), eslint and prettier on the changed files: pass. In the browser, the D01
journey — whose `DELETE` was blocked before — now passes end to end.

**The D04 journey's harness defect.** The `cookie` helper in `e2e/tests/session-journeys.spec.ts`
reads the whole jar (`context.cookies()`) instead of `context.cookies(API_URL)`, which
Playwright filters by URL _path_ and so never listed the refresh cookie scoped to
`/v1/sessions/refresh`. One line, with the reason beside it.

**The browser suite on the branch** (`pnpm test:e2e`, run twice — once after the two fixes
above and again on the final bytes after the `API_PROXY_TARGET` correction below):
**20 of 20 pass** (2.4 and 2.5 min; `w02-proof/d20/e2e-run.log`, `e2e-run-final.log`). That is all
17 existing journeys and the three new ones — D01 (sign-out in one tab clears every tab; the
next person sees only their organizations), D04 (an expired access token is refreshed, the
refresh cookie rotates, a revoked session ends at sign-in) and the refused-refresh journey,
which now exercises the write path its name promises. No `mysqld` and nothing on 3100/3101
left behind.

**The live `next build` witness for D19** — run only after the e2e stack had exited, since
they share `apps/web/.next`; `.next` removed afterwards. Four shapes
(`w02-proof/d20/d19-build-*.log`):

| `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL` | `API_PROXY_TARGET`            | Result                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| absent                     | absent                        | **Refused in the first second**: `PublicConfigError: NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL is not set. A production build has no safe default…`                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `http://localhost:3101`    | absent                        | **Refused**: `…a production build must use https, or "same-origin" with API_PROXY_TARGET.`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `same-origin`              | `http://api.internal.example` | **Refused**: `…a production web server must reach an API on another host over https. Plain http is accepted only for a loopback…`                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| `same-origin`              | `http://127.0.0.1:3101`       | **Builds** (compiled, 9 static pages). Inspected: the call site is inlined as `{nodeEnv:"production",apiBaseUrl:"same-origin",…}`, so the resolver returns `''` and the bundle dials its own origin; the literal `http://localhost:3001` is still present in five chunks as the resolver's development branch, unreachable there (`d19-bundle-inspection.txt`) |

**What the witness found, and the correction.** The first same-origin build was **refused**:
the previous entry's `parseOrigin` held `API_PROXY_TARGET` to the browser's production rules
(https, never loopback), while `.env.example` on the same branch documents
`API_PROXY_TARGET=http://127.0.0.1:4000` — the documented value could not build. The two
readers dial from different places: a loopback compiled into the browser bundle dials the
reader's own machine (D19's point); a loopback in the web server's target is the API on the
same machine, the ordinary case for two Node applications on one host, and plain http is safe
exactly there. Decision (Peter delegated the open decisions on 2026-09-05; recorded): in
production `API_PROXY_TARGET` may be plain http **only when its host is loopback**; a target
on any other host must be https, because that hop carries the session cookies across a
network. `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL`'s rules are unchanged. Changed: `public-config.ts`
(`parseOrigin` takes who dials; the rule and the reason in its comment), the test that held
the target to the browser's rule now asserts the new rule both ways, `.env.example` and
`apps/web/README.md` say it. **Reversal**: `public-config.ts` swapped for the branch's
previous bytes (SHA `63fe5e79…`), **1 of 26 fails** (the loopback target refused), restored by
copy and SHA re-verified (`cfcf29d4…`), **26 of 26**. Whole web unit suite: **23 files, 445
tests**; web typecheck, eslint and prettier: pass (`w02-proof/d20/proxy-target-checks.log`).

**Open, for the reviewer.** (1) `cors.ts` spells the options' shape as a local `CorsPolicy`
interface rather than importing `FastifyCorsOptions`: `@fastify/cors` is
`@nestjs/platform-fastify`'s dependency, not this package's, and Nest's own `CorsOptions`
type is not assignable to it under `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`. No dependency was added.
(2) `@fastify/cors` still writes `Access-Control-Allow-Methods` to a stranger origin; the
browser refuses on the absent `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, which is the gate the test
holds. (3) The loopback-http allowance for the proxy target is a policy call; the trade-off
(no TLS on the intra-machine hop) is the one `50-BOOTSTRAP` §3's single host already makes
for the database.

**Where it lives:** branch `w02-session-browser`, **merged into `master` (`3fed68d`, 2026-09-11)
and pushed** (`next-slices-2026-09-12/UNVERIFIED-FIXES-AUDIT.md`); `master` has since advanced to
`9122b09`. The paragraph that said it was "uncommitted and unpushed on purpose" is historical.
The patch is regenerated as `w02-proof/w02-branch.patch` (its figures and SHA-256 are in
the desk's `result.md`, since a file cannot carry its own hash); per-file hashes in
`w02-proof/fixed-sha256.txt`. The dependency-file flag of the previous entry stands. No
ticket closes: **35/70, 285/583 points (48.9%)**.

## Session/browser slice — D01, D02, D03, D04, D19: built on a branch, proved in units, two browser journeys open

**Findings** (Codex review of 2026-09-05, `CLAUDE-REVIEW-REPORT.md` §4; reviewed revision
`af27739`; D01 and D02 re-probed on `1d89a04`), taken together as the report's §9 step 2
prescribes, because they share one cause: the browser's configuration and its session state
were each handled in several places with several sets of assumptions.

**D01 — sign-out keeps the previous person's cache.** Confirmed at `1d89a04` (probe:
organization and work data retained after the exact `invalidateQueries(['sessions'])`).
Changed: `apps/web/src/lib/auth-boundary.ts` (new) — sign-in, sign-out and an ended session
are announced as events, in this tab and over a same-origin `BroadcastChannel` to the others,
carrying the event name and nothing else; `AuthBoundaryProvider` (new, in the root layout)
cancels every in-flight query, clears the query and mutation caches, and sends the tab to
sign-in when it has no session left; `SessionsScreen` announces instead of invalidating;
`SignInScreen` announces before it navigates. Witness: `tests/auth-boundary.test.tsx` (11) —
the probe inverted, every key gone; a response requested as A that lands after B signed in
does not populate the cache; navigation only on `session-ended` or a remote sign-out;
`tests/session-flow.test.tsx` (+4) — the screens announce, in order, before navigating.

**D02 — default CSRF cookie names disagree.** Confirmed (probe: browser reads
`tm_session_csrf`, server sets `tmanage_session_csrf`). Changed: the default is
`tmanage_session` on both sides — `packages/config` exports `SESSION_COOKIE_NAME_DEFAULT` and
its schema uses it; `apps/web/src/lib/public-config.ts` carries the same value and
`tests/public-config.test.ts` imports both and holds them equal; `e2e/setup/stack.ts` no
longer tells the web app the cookie name, so the suite runs the documented default path.
Witness: Codex's probe re-run against the branch (`w02-proof/probe/review-probes.json`):
`browserReads: tmanage_session_csrf`, `readsServerCookie: true`; in the browser (trace of the
D01 journey) the sign-out request carried `x-csrf-token` read from the default-named cookie.

**D03 — API on a sibling subdomain cannot supply the token.** Confirmed by reading; not
testable here, where two localhost ports share one host. Decision (Peter delegated the open
decisions on 2026-09-05; recorded with its trade-off): the supported production topology is
**same-origin through the web application** — `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL=same-origin` and
`API_PROXY_TARGET`; `next.config.ts` rewrites `/v1/:path*` to the API under the identical
path so the refresh cookie's `Path=/v1/sessions/refresh` still matches. `50-BOOTSTRAP` §3's
two Node applications stay two; the browser sees one. Trade-off: every API byte crosses the
web process (Next's rewrite proxy), which on a shared host is one more hop and one more
memory budget for large downloads that stream through the API — accepted for private alpha,
named for the capacity review. Split origin stays supported only where the API shares the
page's host name (development, e2e); sibling subdomains are documented unsupported
(`apps/web/README.md`, `.env.example`). Also: `ApiClient` keeps the CSRF token the API
returned in memory and prefers it over the cookie, so a tab that signed in can mutate where
the cookie is not readable. Witness: `tests/public-config.test.ts` (rewrite shape, path
identity, both-or-neither rule); `tests/session-recovery.test.ts` (token from sign-in and
from refresh echoed with no cookie readable). **No deployed subdomain pair was tested.**

**D04 — the browser never refreshes.** Confirmed (no caller of `refreshSession` in
`apps/web`). Changed: `ApiClient` (`client.ts`) — a 401 `unauthenticated` on a
session-authenticated request refreshes **once** (coalesced in the tab; serialised across
tabs with `navigator.locks`, because two tabs presenting one refresh token is exactly what
the API's reuse detection revokes a session for) and replays the request **once** — a 401 is
a refusal before the handler ran, so the write was not applied; the refresh's own refusal is
terminal (`onSessionEnded`, once) and the original refusal is thrown; a refresh that never
reaches the API ends nothing; routes that authenticate by password, challenge token or
invitation say `authentication: 'none'` and are never refreshed on. Witness:
`tests/session-recovery.test.ts` (18) — expiry during a read, before a mutation, concurrent
requests, the lock, revoked refresh, network failure, the non-loop, public routes, a client
without recovery.

**D19 — production build silently targets localhost.** Confirmed (`apiBaseUrl()` returned
`http://localhost:3001` under `NODE_ENV=production` with nothing set). Changed:
`public-config.ts` resolves both public values with one set of rules; `next.config.ts` runs
them at load, so `next build` for production **fails in its first second** when the origin is
absent, plain-http, loopback, or carries a path; development keeps `localhost:3001`. Witness:
`tests/public-config.test.ts` (26), including the browser readers through the real
`process.env`. A live `next build` witness was **not** run: it shares `apps/web/.next` with
the e2e stack, which was running when the stop came.

**Reversal proof** (batched; `w02-proof/reversal-run.log`, `restored-run.log`): the seven
production files (`client.ts`, `browser-client.ts`, `session.ts`, `auth.ts`,
`invitations.ts`, `SessionsScreen.tsx`, `SignInScreen.tsx`) swapped for their `1d89a04`
bytes by copy, SHA-256 verified both ways (`reversal-prefix-sha.txt`,
`reversal-fixed-sha.txt`): **16 of 70 fail** — every D01, D02, D03, D04 and D19 witness that
reaches production code; the 54 that pass exercise only the new modules. Restored by copy,
SHA re-verified: **70 of 70**. Whole web unit suite on the branch: **23 files, 445 tests**
(was 21 files, 405; the new 40 are the four files above). Web typecheck, e2e typecheck,
`packages/config` typecheck and tests, eslint over `apps/web`, `packages/config` and `e2e`,
prettier over every changed file: pass (`w02-proof/static-checks-2.log` and the later
re-check). Node 22.22.0 / pnpm 10.15.0 via the Corepack shim, worktree `tmanage-w02`.

**Browser journeys** (`e2e/tests/session-journeys.spec.ts`, new, three journeys; the whole
suite run once on the branch, `w02-proof/e2e-run.log`, 3.0 min): **18 of 20 pass** — all 17
existing journeys with the cookie-name override removed, and the refused-refresh journey.
Two fail, and both are recorded rather than adjusted away:

1. **The D04 idle-return journey — a test-harness defect, not the product.** Its first
   assertion read the refresh cookie through `context.cookies(API_URL)`; Playwright filters
   that list by URL _path_, and the refresh cookie is scoped to `/v1/sessions/refresh`, so it
   is never returned for the origin. Fix: `context.cookies()` with no URL, in the `cookie`
   helper. Nothing after that line ran.
2. **The D01 journey — a newly confirmed API defect, D20.** The browser's
   `DELETE /v1/sessions/current` was refused **before it left the browser**: `Access to fetch
... has been blocked by CORS policy: Method DELETE is not allowed by
Access-Control-Allow-Methods in preflight response` (console line in
   `w02-proof/e2e-failures/…4eb88…/trace.zip`; the request shows status −1 with the CSRF
   header present and no cookies attached). `apps/api/src/main.ts`'s `enableCors` names
   origins and headers but not methods, and the adapter's default does not include `DELETE`.
   Consequence at `1d89a04`, unchanged by this slice: **on any split-origin deployment the
   browser cannot sign out and cannot remove a factor** (`disableFactor` is the other
   `DELETE`); no existing journey sent a `DELETE` from a page, which is why it was never seen.
   In the same-origin topology no preflight exists and the route works. Candidate fix, one
   line in `main.ts` — `methods: ['GET', 'HEAD', 'POST', 'PUT', 'PATCH', 'DELETE']` — **not
   applied**: the API is outside this slice's owned paths and the stop came first. Carried as
   **D20** (P1 on split origin, moot on same origin) for the next slice, with the journey as
   its ready witness. The passing refused-refresh journey is therefore weaker than its name:
   its `DELETE` was CORS-blocked too, and the tab reached sign-in through the read path's
   refresh refusal, not the write's; it is re-read after D20 lands.

**Not done here, on purpose or by the stop:** the API `methods` line (D20); a live
`next build` witness for D19; the D04 journey re-run after its one-line test fix; a real
subdomain pair for D03; proactive refresh before expiry (reactive-on-401 satisfies the
acceptance list; a timer is an optimisation); a client-side link to the sessions screen (it
is reachable only by URL — D12's family).

**Where it lives:** branch `w02-session-browser`, worktree `tmanage-w02`, cut from
`1d89a04`, **since merged into `master` (`3fed68d`, 2026-09-11) and pushed**. The paragraph that
stood here described it as "uncommitted and unpushed on purpose" under the 2026-09-05 parallel
arrangement, in which Codex was reviewer and default integrator; that arrangement ended on
2026-09-06 17:44 and the sentence is historical. The patch (`w02-branch.patch`, 24 files, +1,899
−49), hashes, logs, probe output and the two failure traces are under
`C:/Users/Peter/Documents/ChatGPT/TManage/w02-proof/`. The branch touches
`apps/web/package.json` and `pnpm-lock.yaml` (a dev-dependency on `@tmanage/config` for one
test; workspace link only, `pnpm install --offline` resolved it) — a dependency file, flagged
for the integrator. It adds sections at the top of this file, as `w01-scanner-cleanup` does;
the two insertions are independent. No ticket closes: **35/70, 285/583 points (48.9%)**;
these are repairs inside WEB-001, ID-002 and the deployment profile.

## FILE-002 slice C — the download gate and the views, built and proved against the filesystem driver

Built in the same session as slice B's completion, on a green chain (`631e092`). A read-only
fleet of seventeen (run `wf_1aca4f71-dcb`: twelve readers over the domain predicate, the
views, the repository, the contracts, the e2e stack, the planning documents and the HTTP
conventions; four adversarial lenses; one synthesizer) mapped the slice before a line was
written. Peter raised the agent cap to 30 for that fleet and put it back to 10 the same
evening; the cap is 10. **FILE-002 closes with this slice, and the loop it closes cannot run in
production.** Every gate below was executed with `STORAGE_DRIVER=filesystem`.
`storage.module.ts` wires `UnavailableObjectStore` for `s3` — every method rejects with
`ObjectStoreUnavailableError` — and `packages/config` refuses `filesystem` under
`NODE_ENV=production`. There is therefore **no working object store in any production
configuration**, and upload, version, approval and download are inoperable there until
**FILE-003** builds the R2 driver. The refusal is deliberate and honest; the consequence is that
this slice's proof is a proof about development and e2e, not about the product a user would touch.

### What the fleet found, and what changed because of it

- **`isServable` had no caller and one argument.** `packages/domain` checked the status
  alone; the verdict's _value_ and the zone were nowhere in the domain package. Built:
  `isServableVersion({ status, scanVerdict, trustZone })` — `ready`, `clean`, `private`,
  together — on the values as the row carries them. 0019's trigger guards the transition
  into `ready`; this guards the read, because a replacement version (`23` §10) is born in
  quarantine under an asset that is already `ready`.
- **Two reads describe two moments.** `findById` then `findLatestVersion` (the completion
  view's shape) can straddle a promotion. Built: `findWithLatestVersion` — one statement, the
  asset `LEFT JOIN` its greatest `version_no` in its own organization.
- **The client's relation is the request row, never the asset alone.** An internal upload
  carries no client organization, so `authorize()`'s rule 7 is a no-op on it; a sibling
  client organization sharing the project would have read an internal upload. Built: for a
  client, the request named by `object_id` must exist, sit in the asset's project and belong
  to the principal's client organization, before `authorize()` is even asked.
- **`lifecycle: 'active'` was fixed on purpose in FILE-001's write path** and would have
  been wrong on the read path: rule 6 lets an internal principal read an archived project's
  file and lets no client. Built: the project's true lifecycle from its row.
- **The zone is a literal.** `openObject({ zone: 'private' })`, never `version.trustZone`
  passed through — the row must _say_ private (the predicate) and the code must _open_
  private; a row that lied would fail the read rather than steer it. The size is held to the
  row's before the first byte, as the scanner's read is. ADR-0006's sentence "reads it from
  the row and never from a zone literal" is corrected there to this rule.
- **The two doors' views were one type.** `FileAssetView` served the _declared_ MIME to
  everyone and no rejection to anyone. Built: the detected type once the verifier has one;
  `rejectionCode` on the studio's view (TM-15, `22` :153) and a `ClientFileAssetView` without
  it (`12-PERMISSION-MATRIX` §39: security metadata) — `35` :100's copy is the client's,
  and the studio sees the code, never the engine's detection name.
- **Every refusal is one 404.** Not found, another tenant's, another client's, still
  `scanning`, `rejected`, a quarantine-only latest version, a missing or truncated private
  object: byte-identical bodies but for the per-request correlation id; the cause lives on a
  `file_asset.downloaded` `denied` row's `audit_code` alone. A polling client writes denied
  rows — `27` SEC-10's mass-download evidence is worth the rows (decision D6).
- **The proxied stream is the first streaming route** in `apps/api`. `StreamableFile` keeps
  Nest in its own response mode (the exception filter and the interceptors still shape
  everything that is not the bytes); the `ClientProjectionInterceptor` lets a
  `StreamableFile` through **by name** rather than walking a stream's internals — the walk
  finds nothing today, and a property on the stream would have turned a download into a 500.
- **No planning line fixes the response headers.** Recorded as decision D2: `attachment`
  always (never `inline` — `26` §5's polyglots and content-disposition XSS), the detected
  type, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Cache-Control: private, no-store` (`27` SEC-05),
  `Content-Length`, no `ETag`. The filename has an ASCII fallback with quotes, backslashes,
  semicolons, separators and control bytes replaced, and an RFC 5987 `filename*` for the
  real name.
- **What the fleet could not establish, settled by reading:** `malware_detected` _is_ written
  to `rejection_code` by the scanner (its enum has four codes, not three); no contract
  harness validates `contracts/events/*.schema.json`, and the contracts live under
  `docs/planning/`, which this repository never edits — so the OpenAPI and event-schema
  divergences are recorded, not fixed.

### Decisions taken under Peter's delegation

- **D1 — proxy, not a signed URL.** Membership is re-resolved on every request (`27`
  AUTH-12); the bootstrap target is one proxied Node process anyway (50-BOOTSTRAP). The
  signed-URL twin of the part route is the paid-beta option, and it would need a principal
  in the token and a re-check at redemption.
- **D2 — the headers**, above. Previews and inline rendering are CL-03's and SEC-12's.
- **D3 — a client downloads request attachments only**, held to the request row.
- **D4 — `rejectionCode` is never on the client's view**; `35` :100's copy is theirs. This
  overturns the earlier "rejectionCode yes" note in the FILE-002 plan; recorded.
- **D5 — no uploader carve-out** before `ready`.
- **D6 — a denied row for every refusal**, the not-yet-ready ones included.
- **D7 — the correlation id in the client's copy** is read from the rejection audit row
  when the portal shows it (a later ticket); no column added.

## FILE-002 slice B — scanning and promotion, built and proved

Built across two sessions on 2026-09-05: the first stopped at Peter's request at 44% of its
context with the work committed as `217c415` and honestly labelled _not green, nothing
proven_; this one (after the thirty-sixth reconciliation) took the suite from 13 of 15 to
15 of 15, proved nine fixes by reversal, and ran the chain. Peter's delegation of F1–F5
stands as recorded under slice A; this slice takes F1 (ADR-0006), F2 and F3 to code.

### The plan refuted first

A read-only fleet of ten (run `wf_33acafb7-110`) re-read the slice B plan against the code,
the trigger, the storage port, clamd's protocol and the planning documents before a line was
written. Its refutations are the design; each is now a built control and a test case:

- **D1 — a second read is a second chance.** The plan copied the sealed quarantine object
  after a clean verdict. Built instead: **one read, teed** — the same stream feeds the
  sha256, the scanner and a streamed promotion sink under the same key in `private`; the
  digest is held to `content_hash` before anything is committed. The bytes in `private` are
  the bytes the scanner saw, by construction (ADR-0006).
- **D2 — the orphan.** A pass that seals the private object and dies before its transaction
  leaves a servable object under a row that says `quarantine`. Built: `ObjectStore.withdraw`,
  the one undo; it runs after every rejection and when a pass loses a dispute to a standing
  `infected`, and never when the row is `ready` (same bytes).
- **D3 — "any clean version" is not "the latest".** `23` §10's replacement creates a new
  version; a clean first version must not vouch for an unscanned second. 0019's trigger
  binds `ready` to the version with the greatest `version_no`, in the asset's own
  organization — the schema's first cross-table trigger, org-filtered like every read (D13).
- **D4 — `unscanned` churn.** Under `none` the plan re-recorded `unscanned` every tick.
  Built: the selection skips a version already `unscanned` unless the driver is an engine
  (`rescanUnscanned`), and the write itself is conditional on `NULL` — two `none` passes
  record it once, with one `scan_failed` row (`no_scanner`).
- **D6 — starvation.** Without a claim, one object that always fails is scanned first every
  pass and the rest wait behind it for ever. Built: `claimForScan` (a conditional UPDATE,
  `scan_claimed_at`, optimistic on `version`), the claim left standing on failure so the row
  waits out `STALE_SCAN_CLAIM_MS` (decision 13, fifteen minutes), then a bound of
  `MAX_CONSECUTIVE_FAILURES` (5) per pass, after which the pass stops and leaves the rest
  unclaimed.
- **D7 — the stub's per-chunk search misses a split signature.** Built: a rolling window
  that carries the last `EICAR.length - 1` bytes of each chunk into the next comparison.
- **D8/D9 — clamd.** INSTREAM over `node:net`: 4-byte big-endian length frames, a zero
  frame to finish, `OK` / `FOUND` / `ERROR` parsed exactly and anything else a protocol
  error; a connect timeout (5 s) apart from the per-object timeout
  (`MALWARE_SCAN_TIMEOUT_MS`); `probe` (PING → PONG) before any row is claimed, so an
  unreachable engine stops the pass without a claim; the consecutive-failure breaker above.
- **D10 — the triple is pinned as a unit.** `scan_verdict`, `scanned_at`, `scanner` are
  write-once together (0019), `unscanned` the one replaceable value; a verdict never loses its
  time or its scanner, and never goes back to `NULL`.
- **D11 — the detection name is a fingerprint of the engine.** It goes to stderr only
  (`onDetection`), keyed by asset id and correlation id; the row, the audit metadata and the
  event carry `malware_detected` and nothing the engine said.
- **D12 — the machine checks presence, not value.** `FileAssetsRepository.transition`
  refuses `ready` unless `scanVerdict === 'clean'` before any write; 0019's trigger refuses
  it again at the engine.
- **C4 — one correlation id per asset**, minted by the verifier and by the scanner, so the
  `scanned` row and `file.ready.v1` for one asset share it and two assets never do.

### What was built

| Piece                                  | Where                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| -------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **`ObjectStore.promote` / `withdraw`** | `packages/storage`: `promote` opens a staging sink beside the destination in `private` under the **same key** (`<key>.<random>.tmp`), counts and md5s what it is fed; `commit` closes, holds the byte count to the size the row says, and renames — the same atomic seal `completeMultipart` makes; `abort` closes quietly (a write in flight makes the file stream emit `ERR_STREAM_DESTROYED`, waited on by hand) and removes the staging file. Fake and filesystem drivers, one-shot handles (`PromotionClosedError`). 54 storage tests                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| **The scanner port**                   | `apps/api/src/common/scan/`: `MalwareScanner` with `kind: 'none' \| 'engine'`, `probe`, `scan(stream, size)`; `NoneScanner`, `StubScanner` (the EICAR rolling window), `ClamavScanner` (INSTREAM, D8/D9), `ScannerModule.forConfig / forScanner / none`. `MALWARE_SCAN_DRIVER` gains `none` as a legal production value (F3), `CLAMAV_HOST` required for `clamav`, `CLAMAV_PORT` defaults 3310                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **The pass**                           | `file-scanner.ts`: probe first; per organization, per row — claim, open, size held before reading, one stream teed three ways, digest held to `content_hash`; **clean** → commit → one transaction {`recordScan`, `scanning → ready` with the verdict, `file_asset.scanned` (`allowed`), `file.ready.v1`}; **infected** → abort → one transaction {`recordScan`, `scanning → rejected` (`malware_detected`), `file_asset.rejected` (`denied`), `file.rejected.v1`} → `withdraw`; **none** → `unscanned` once, no claim, `scan_failed` `no_scanner`; **failure** → the claim stands, `scan_failed` with the cause; a standing verdict that differs → `file_asset.scan_disputed`. `verify.ts` runs the verifier then the scanner — no new cron command |
| **Migration 0019**                     | `scan_verdict`, `scanned_at`, `scanner`, `trust_zone` on `file_versions`; `scan_claimed_at` on `file_assets`; the write-once triple with the `unscanned` exception; `trust_zone` `quarantine → private` only with `clean`, **NULL-safe (`<=>`)** — `NEW.scan_verdict = 'clean'` is NULL for a verdict-less row and `IF NOT (NULL)` would have let the move through; a `BEFORE INSERT` "born in quarantine, without a verdict" trigger; the latest-version `ready` trigger. `schema.ts` mirrored                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| **Repository, domain, audit**          | `FileAssetsRepository.listAwaitingScan`, `organizationsAwaitingScan` (bootstrap hatch), `claimForScan`, `recordScan`, the `ready` value guard in `transition`; `file.ready.v1` in `packages/domain`; audit actions `file_asset.scanned` (must be `allowed` — the third such rule in `AuditEventsRepository`) and `file_asset.scan_disputed`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

### Decisions taken under Peter's delegation

- **F1 — the trust zone is a column; the key is stable across zones.** ADR-0006. Promotion
  is streamed, not copied; the object exists twice until FILE-003 deletes the quarantine
  copy of a `ready` version (H5 — kept for reconciliation).
- **F3 — `none` is honest, and its consequence is stated plainly: under
  `MALWARE_SCAN_DRIVER=none` no upload ever becomes downloadable.** Every asset parks at
  `scanning` with `unscanned` on its version; a real scanner later replaces the verdict and
  the asset moves. `scanning → expired` stays the machine's unused edge — door 8 (no exit on
  a permanent outage) is now one state later than it was, and still open.
- **D14 — the API identity writes to `private`.** The bucket-policy split (`49` :72's
  separate identity, F2) is the paid-beta follow-up, recorded in the ADR.
- **H5 — the duplicate object** is accepted for reconciliation rather than deleted at
  commit.
- Decision 13's fifteen minutes is the scan claim's bound too; the failure bound is five.

### What went wrong between the two sessions

`217c415` shipped with **stale `dist/` in `packages/storage` and `packages/config`**: the
quiet-close `abort` and the `none`-in-production config were in source and not in the build
the api reads. The two red cases (a `.tmp` staging file left in `private` after a hash
mismatch; an overlapping pass whose rejection counted as a failure) were both the old
`abort` throwing `ERR_STREAM_DESTROYED`. Rebuilding the three packages made the suite 15 of
15 with no source change. The rule stands and is repeated here: **`pnpm --filter <pkg> build`
after touching `packages/*`, before any api suite is believed.**

## FILE-002 planned, not built — the fleet's map, the doors, and the decisions that are Peter's

Read after the completing claim landed, on a green chain with nothing owed. USAGE-001 slices
2–5 are blocked on questions 7 and 8 (the ledger's shape is a P0-contract question, the
usage read's capability has no name), so FILE-002 — `28` row "verification/hash/MIME/scan
state worker, 13 → split" — is the next unblocked ticket. Six read-only readers (run
`wf_44df7122-fd1`: the pack, the worker and its queue, the storage package, the assets and
versions, this record, and one adversarial lens) mapped it with about a hundred `path:line`
cites; the full output is in the run's `journal.jsonl`. **Nothing was written to the tree.**
The next session refutes every cited line before building, as the sweeper session did.

### What the pack demands, as read

- `23` §10 is one sentence: `created → uploading → uploaded → verifying → scanning → ready |
rejected | expired | cancelled`, "file is inaccessible outside upload owner/authorized
  processing until `ready`". Nothing defines `verifying` against `scanning`; `03` §108
  ("worker verifies checksum, MIME, size, malware scan … unscanned uploads are quarantined")
  and `26`'s DFD (one verification job, one combined check node, `safe → ready`, `unsafe →
rejected + security event`) are the only semantics.
- `24` §4 has exactly three file rows: `upload.completed.v1` (consumer: "verification/scan
  worker"), `file.ready.v1` ("validation/scan passed", audit: security metadata) and
  `file.rejected.v1` ("validation/scan failed", audit: yes). No `upload.verified`, no
  `scan.*`, no payload minimums for any of the three. `24` §7: never raw content; §65: usage
  events carry no filename.
- `49` §4: three buckets by trust state, and **two different key layouts** — quarantine
  `…/upload/{upload_uuid}/…`, private `…/asset/{asset_uuid}/version/{version_uuid}/{safe_name}`.
  §73: "quarantine and preview workers have separate least-privilege identities." §5: a
  rejected object's bytes are still an "uploaded source object" and §108 reduces usage only
  after provider deletion is confirmed — so a rejected file stays counted until FILE-003
  deletes it. That is the document's answer, not a question.
- `26` §79 and `27` SEC-06: signature allowlist, spoofed MIME, SVG/HTML, polyglot, archive
  bomb, forced safe disposition, quarantine. `50` §39: malware scanning is feature-flagged or
  conservative in private alpha.

### What the code has, and what it lacks

| Has                                                                                                                                                                                                                          | Lacks                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The machine in `packages/domain` with the facts each edge requires (`verifying → scanning` needs `contentHash`, `detectedMimeType`; `→ rejected` needs `rejectionCode`; `scanning → ready` needs `scanVerdict`, `scannedAt`) | Any caller of `isServable` — the "only `ready` may be served" rule is documentation; SEC-001 filters field names, not status                                                                                                                            |
| `file_versions.content_hash`, `detected_mime_type`, `file_assets.rejection_code` — NULL, written by nothing; `upload_sessions.declared_content_hash` written and compared to nothing                                         | Any column for `scan_verdict`, `scanned_at`, the scanner, or the **trust zone** — `zone: 'quarantine'` is a literal at four call sites and no row says where an object is                                                                               |
| `FileAssetsRepository.transition`, conditional on the status it leaves                                                                                                                                                       | It discards `facts`: `rejectionCode` would pass the machine and never reach the column. No `recordVerification` on a version at all                                                                                                                     |
| `ObjectStore`: begin, complete, abort — and its header arguing that a `getObject` nobody has a rule for is an escape hatch                                                                                                   | Read, head, copy, promote, delete. A sealed object is unreadable and **undeletable** through the port; the composite etag is `md5(concat(part digests))-N`, not a hash of the bytes, so SHA-256 means a second pass                                     |
| The worker: at-least-once outbox handlers inside the batch transaction, `afterCommit` effects at-most-once                                                                                                                   | Any grant on `file_assets` or `file_versions` for `tmanage_worker`; any storage driver in the worker; `tmanage_app` has INSERT only on `file_versions` ("the grant arrives with the code that writes them", `users.sql`)                                |
| `MALWARE_SCAN_DRIVER` in `packages/config` (`stub` \| `clamav`, 30 s timeout)                                                                                                                                                | An honest bootstrap value: production refuses `stub` and there is no `none`, so the first production boot must either lie (`clamav` pointed at nothing) or fail. A config bug, recorded here                                                            |
| `trg_file_versions_immutable` pins organization, asset, `object_key`, `size_bytes`                                                                                                                                           | The repository header and 0015 §107 both say the trigger refuses every UPDATE; it does not — only the missing grant does. Both comments become false with the first grant and must be corrected in the same change (0015's in a new migration's header) |

### The doors the adversarial lens found

1. **Promotion is structurally impossible as specified.** `49` §4's two layouts need the
   key to change; the trigger forbids it. The safe choice is a `trust_zone` column on
   `file_versions` with the key **stable across zones** (the driver already lays every zone
   out under the same key), promotion a copy under an unchanged key — recorded as a
   divergence from `49` §4 by ADR, because the alternative is a mutable key.
2. **A network call inside the outbox batch.** Hashing, sniffing, a 30 s scanner round-trip
   and a copy do not belong inside the relay's transaction (row locks across the network) nor
   in `afterCommit` (at-most-once, unretryable). The split the ticket asks for is along the
   transaction boundary: the state moves are transactional and conditional; the work runs in
   a pass over `file_assets` by status — the sweeper's shape, stale-claim reclaim included.
3. **The audit validator refuses a media type.** `VALUE_PATTERN` admits no `/` or `+`, so
   `image/svg+xml` throws `UnsafeAuditMetadataError`; `signature` and `reason` are forbidden
   key segments. Record the detected type as a token (`application_pdf`), the rejection under
   `rejection_code`, and never widen the pattern. Three catalog actions: `file_asset.verified`
   (allowed), `file_asset.rejected` (denied — §12's "denied sensitive attempt"),
   `file_asset.scan_failed` (error). A SHA-256 hex digest is exactly the 64-character cap.
4. **A rejected object is evidence.** It stays in quarantine, is never promoted, never
   deleted by the verification job, and its bytes stay counted (`49` §5/§108 above); deletion
   is FILE-003's privileged, time-bounded job. A malware finding is recorded as a token, never
   the scanner's free text.
5. **Redelivery must be a no-op, and a verdict must be unrewritable.** Conditional writes
   (`… WHERE content_hash IS NULL`) and a trigger that pins `content_hash` and `scan_verdict`
   once set, so a second delivery cannot change a recorded verdict even if a guard is
   forgotten.
6. **A late PUT during verification.** The public part route is session-blind; the manifest
   is the revocation and the driver removes it at completion, so a sealed object cannot be
   altered — but the S3 driver (FILE-003) must presign `UploadPart`, never `PutObject`, or
   every minted URL outlives the seal and hash-then-promote becomes a TOCTOU. Written into the
   port's contract before the adapter exists.
7. **The gate.** `FileAssetView.status` is raw and the view carries the _declared_ MIME.
   Until `ready` exists, a client sees a `scanning` or `rejected` asset exactly like a ready
   one; FILE-002 gives `isServable` its first caller and decides what a client DTO shows
   (`rejectionCode` yes, hashes and scanner no).
8. **No exit from `verifying`.** The machine has no `verifying → expired`, no
   `uploaded → expired`, and `ready`/`rejected` are terminal — a parked event or a dead pass
   leaves an asset mid-pipeline with its bytes counted. A stale-`verifying` re-run (the
   conditional final transition is the guard) needs no new edge; a permanent outage does.

### The split, as this session would build it

- **Slice A — verification, in the API.** `verify:once` beside `sweep:once` on the same tick:
  organizations holding `uploaded` assets (bootstrap read, its own reason string), then per
  organization `uploaded → verifying` (the machine's conditional move as the claim), one pass
  over the object — SHA-256 and the first bytes' signature in the same stream — compared with
  `declared_content_hash` when one was given, then in one transaction `recordVerification`
  (conditional on NULL), `verifying → scanning` with the facts written, or `→ rejected` with
  `rejection_code` (`hash_mismatch`, `type_not_allowed`, `type_mismatch`), the audit row, and
  `file.rejected.v1`. A signature allowlist in code (PDF, PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, ZIP-family
  for the Office types, textual for `text/plain|csv|markdown`; SVG and HTML refused as active
  content, `27` SEC-06). Needs: `ObjectStore.openObject` (the port's header rewritten, a stub
  on `UnavailableObjectStore`, real bytes in the suite via `forLocalStore`), `UPDATE` on
  `file_versions` for the credential that runs the pass, a migration recreating
  `trg_file_versions_immutable` to pin `content_hash` / `detected_mime_type` once set (and
  correcting 0015's "immutable by construction"), the repository projecting facts to columns.
  Nothing is promoted and nothing becomes `ready` in slice A.
- **Slice B — scanning and promotion.** `scan_verdict`, `scanned_at`, `scanner`, `trust_zone`
  columns; a scanner port with an honest `none` driver that records `unscanned` and does
  **not** mark `ready` unless a documented profile says so; `ObjectStore.promote` defined for
  copy semantics; `scanning → ready` + `file.ready.v1`; the client gate. Blocked on decisions
  F1–F4 below.
- **Slice C — the gate and the views**, with FILE-003's download path.

### Decisions for Peter (numbered on from USAGE-001's twelve)

- **F1. The trust zone is a column and the key is stable** across zones — a divergence from
  `49` §4's two layouts, by ADR. Recommend yes; the alternative relaxes the immutability
  trigger.
- **F2. Who verifies.** The pass in the API under `tmanage_app` with one new `UPDATE` grant
  (the sweeper's precedent, decision 10), or a fourth database user for the quarantine worker
  as `49` §73 asks. Recommend the API pass for the bootstrap profile, recorded as a divergence
  with the fourth user as the paid-beta follow-up.
- **F3. Scanning in the bootstrap profile.** `50` §39 allows conservative or flagged scanning;
  `packages/config` has no honest value. Recommend `MALWARE_SCAN_DRIVER=none` as a real
  member that records `unscanned` and leaves the asset at `scanning` — never `ready` — until
  a scanner exists, with the bootstrap profile document saying so; the alternative (ready
  while unscanned, recorded) is a product call.
- **F4. Rejected bytes stay counted** until FILE-003 deletes them (`49` §5/§108). Recommend
  following the document; recorded so it is not a surprise on a bill.
- **F5. Slice A's allowlist** — the seven families above, SVG and HTML refused. Recommend
  yes; a wider list is one edit in one file.

## The completing claim — the carried race closed, the claim reaped, the silent abort named

The one item that had been carried through four sessions — a completion still talking to the
provider while a cancel, a second completion or a sweep moved its row — is closed. Designed
first with a read-only fleet of six (run `wf_c173e07e-bd6`: the contract surface, the test
suites, the migrator, the planning docs, the sweeper and the audit catalog, and one
adversarial lens on the new state), then built, then proved by seven reversals. Peter's
standing instruction was the brief: nothing may slip because a decision made things easier.
The fleet found three places where the naive claim would have.

### What the claim is

`upload_sessions.status` gains **`completing`** — migration `0017_upload_session_completing.sql`,
`UPLOAD_SESSION_STATUSES`, and the repository header. A completion moves its row
`reserved → completing` in its own short transaction **before** `completeMultipart` is called;
from then until it settles, that request is the one thing that can move the row:

- **Cancel** finds `completing` and answers **409 `conflict`** (`completion_in_flight`,
  message "the upload is being completed; wait for it to finish", no `version` field, so the
  web client renders the API's words rather than its version-conflict banner) — checked
  _before_ `releaseAs`, because on that path the provider abort runs ahead of the status
  guard and would have abandoned an upload the provider was assembling.
- **A second completion** of the same session answers the same 409.
- **A replay of the key** answers 409 with "whose completion is in flight; wait for it" —
  _not_ "use a new key": a client that followed that advice would open a second reservation
  and a second provider upload for the same bytes.
- **The sweeper** never selects it: `listExpired` is `status = 'reserved'`, unchanged.
- **The open-upload cap** counts it: `countReservedFor` became `countOpenFor` over
  `reserved | completing`. Without that a person at the cap held the cap-th plus every
  completion they could keep in flight (the fleet's door 5).
- **The view** still reports `reservedBytes` under a claim (the bytes are held) and withholds
  the part targets (they are a bearer credential for a write; the claim is when the object is
  being assembled from them).

Every exit settles the claim, and `from` is explicit at every transition — never a widened
default, so exactly one status→status edge exists per release path and a double release is
unreachable by construction (the counter's guard is organization-wide and would not catch
one): `completing → completed` in the commit transaction; `completing → failed` for a lost
upload or a wrong size, through `releaseAs(…, { from: ['completing'] })`; and **`completing →
reserved`** — the one backward edge — in a `finally`, for everything else: a part the client
can re-send (FILE-001b decision 11 stands, its two cases green), a provider outage, a refused
abort, a commit that did not go through. A claim never outlives its request.

### The door the naive claim would have opened, and its reaper

A process that dies between the claim and the `finally` leaves a row `completing` for good:
complete and cancel answer 409, expiry does not see it, the bytes stay counted, and one of
the opener's capped slots stays taken. The fleet's verdict — "shipping the claim without a
reaper is strictly worse than not claiming" — was right, and the sweeper's pass now has a
second door: `listStaleClaims` selects `completing` rows whose `updated_at` is older than
**`STALE_CLAIM_MS` (fifteen minutes)**, `FilesService.reclaim` returns each to `reserved`
(bound to its context as `expire` is), and the expiry in the same pass then takes it if it is
also past the cutoff. The reclaim releases nothing itself; a reclaimed row still inside its
lifetime waits for its opener or for expiry like any other. `organizationsHoldingExpired`
finds an organization by either condition. The report gains `reclaimed`; the parsed line
appends "N claim(s) reclaimed" only when non-zero, so `e2e/setup/stack.ts` reads it as before.
**USAGE-001 decision 12: the bound is fifteen minutes, one edit in `upload-session-sweeper.ts`,
Peter's to change.** The trade is stated in the file: too short undercuts a slow assembly
(that one row's race reopened, no more); too long holds a dead claim's bytes and slot.

One clock note, learned from a red test: `updated_at` is stamped by the application pool's
session, pinned to `+00:00`, and compared against the host clock, as `expires_at` is. The
suite's helper must date a claim from a bound `Date`, never from the admin connection's
`current_timestamp` — that pool's server clock is `SYSTEM`, hours off on this machine.

### The silent abort, named

The completion-refusal path (`releaseAs … 'best-effort'`) now records
**`upload_session.abort_failed`** when the provider refuses to abandon an upload it has
already lost: `error`, `objectId` the session, `provider_upload_id`, `cause`, the refusal's
name (`MultipartUploadNotFoundError`), the project and the declared bytes — in its own
best-effort transaction, as the create path's row is. The catalog comment names both
producers. The last of the review's low findings is closed.

### Why 0017 is a migration when the column admits the value already

`status` is a `VARCHAR(32)` with no ENUM and no CHECK, and 0015's header — which enumerates
five values — is frozen by the migrator's checksum, so it is amended in 0017's header (the
0016 precedent) and not in place. A comment-only file is refused by the migrator ("contains
no statements"), so 0017 rewrites the column with a `COMMENT` naming all six values — same
type, same NOT NULL, no DEFAULT, both indexes and 0016's trigger untouched — because
`SHOW CREATE TABLE` is what an operator reads, not `schema.ts`. **Deployment: one migration
to apply.** The ledger migration the USAGE-001 plan named `0017` becomes `0018`.

### What the fleet flagged and this session did not change

- **Provider succeeded, commit failed** (the fleet's door 9). The `finally` returns the row to
  `reserved`; the retry re-calls `completeMultipart`, the filesystem driver has already sealed
  the object and removed the manifest, so the retry is `upload_not_found` → `failed`, the
  bytes go back, and the sealed object is an orphan no version names. **The same orphan as
  before the claim** (then: `reserved` until expiry, same object), reached by the client's
  retry rather than the sweeper. The fix is a probe of the destination before the retry, or
  a record of the sealed object's etag on the row — FILE-003's orphan lifecycle, carried.
- **A PUT during the assembly** (door 7). The part targets are withdrawn from the view under a
  claim, but a client that already holds them can PUT through the public route, which has no
  session to consult, until the driver removes the manifest at the end of `completeMultipart`.
  The window is the driver's, existed before the claim, and stays recorded; a session lookup on
  the public parts route would undo its stated no-tenant design.
- **No session state machine in `packages/domain`** (door 10): the illegality lives in the
  explicit `from` at every `transition` call, and the repository's `transition` doc says so.
